m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a Colab notebook in your Google Drive and run a code cell.
  • Switch the runtime to a T4 GPU and confirm it with nvidia-smi and torch.cuda.is_available().
  • Know what Colab's free tier gives you and what it holds back.
  • Recover when Colab refuses a GPU, forgets your variables, or says the GPU is idle.

Training a neural network is mostly matrix multiplication. Multiplying two 4096 × 4096 matrices takes 2 × 4096³, about 137 billion, multiply-and-add operations. NVIDIA rates the T4, the GPU that Google Colab lends to free users, at roughly 8 trillion 32-bit floating-point operations per second at peak. Even at half that speed, the whole multiplication finishes in a few hundredths of a second. The two-core CPU that Colab gives you without a GPU is many times slower.

The networks in Modules 2 to 4 are small enough that a CPU handles them in seconds. From Module 5 on, you'll train convolutional networks on real image datasets, and that's where the GPU turns a long wait into a short one. Setting it up now, while nothing depends on it, means you'll already know how it behaves when it matters.

#What you need

  • A Google account. Some schools switch Colab off for student accounts. If Colab says you don't have access, use a personal account instead.
  • A recent browser: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, or Edge.
  • Nothing to install. Colab's machines come with PyTorch, torchvision, NumPy, scikit-learn, and matplotlib already installed.

The free tier costs nothing, and it makes no promises. Which GPU you get, and for how long, depends on demand and on how much you've used recently. Google doesn't publish the exact limits. Every exercise in this course is sized to fit comfortably inside them.

#Step 1: make a notebook and run a cell

  1. Go to colab.research.google.com (opens in a new tab) and sign in.
  2. In the window that opens, click New notebook. If no window appears, use File › New notebook in Drive.
  3. Click the name Untitled0.ipynb at the top left and rename it dlcv-setup.ipynb.
  4. Click in the empty code cell, type print("hello from Colab"), and press Shift + Enter.

The first run takes several seconds because Colab is starting a machine for you. When it's ready, the Connect button at the top right turns into small RAM and Disk meters, and your text prints under the cell. The notebook file itself is saved in a folder called Colab Notebooks in your Google Drive.

Your code doesn't run in the browser. It runs on a virtual machine in a Google data center, and the browser only shows you the results. Hold on to that picture; it explains nearly every surprise in this lesson.

#Step 2: switch the runtime to a GPU

  1. Open Runtime › Change runtime type.
  2. Under Hardware accelerator, choose T4 GPU.
  3. Click Save.

Saving gives you a brand-new machine with a GPU attached. Anything the old machine had in memory is gone, so change the runtime type before you run real work, not halfway through it.

#Step 3: prove the GPU is there

Two checks, one asking NVIDIA's driver and one asking PyTorch. In a new cell, run the driver's status tool. In Colab you type a shell command with an exclamation mark in front, so the cell reads !nvidia-smi:

It prints a table. The version numbers and temperature will differ, but the important part looks like this:

That says one GPU (number 0), a Tesla T4, using 0 of its roughly 15 GB of memory. Now ask PyTorch:

The output above was made by the machine that builds this page, which has no NVIDIA GPU, so it says False and skips the last line. That's also exactly what you'll see in Colab if you forgot Step 2. With the T4 attached, you should see:

The xs stand for whatever versions Colab has installed this term. The +cu part means this copy of PyTorch was built for CUDA, NVIDIA's platform for running general code on its GPUs. torch.cuda.is_available() is the line you'll lean on for the rest of the course.

#Your keyboard and the local-install question

Colab works the same in every browser. The differences are the shortcut keys and whether installing PyTorch on your own computer makes sense.

Windows

  • Ctrl + Enter runs the current cell; Shift + Enter runs it and moves to the next one.
  • Ctrl + M, then B, adds a code cell below. Tools › Keyboard shortcuts lists the rest.
  • A local install only gets you a GPU if your PC has an NVIDIA graphics card. If it does, the selector at pytorch.org/get-started/locally builds the right pip command for your CUDA version. Stick with Colab for this course unless you already know you want this.

macOS

  • Cmd + Enter runs the current cell; Shift + Enter runs it and moves to the next one.
  • Cmd + M, then B, adds a code cell below. Tools › Keyboard shortcuts lists the rest.
  • Macs don't have NVIDIA GPUs, so torch.cuda.is_available() is always False on a Mac. Apple silicon Macs have their own GPU backend called mps, which this course doesn't rely on. Use Colab for the GPU modules.

Chromebook

  • Ctrl + Enter runs the current cell; Shift + Enter runs it and moves to the next one.
  • Ctrl + M, then B, adds a code cell below. Tools › Keyboard shortcuts lists the rest.
  • Chromebooks have no CUDA GPU, and school-managed ones usually can't install software. Colab in Chrome is the whole setup, and it's all this course needs.

#Fixes for the four problems people actually hit

"Cannot connect to GPU backend." Colab shows this when you've used up your recent GPU allowance or none are free. Switch to CPU in Runtime › Change runtime type and keep going: every lesson through Module 4 runs comfortably on a CPU. Try the GPU again later, often the next day.

torch.cuda.is_available() still prints False. The runtime is still a CPU one, or you changed it and are looking at the old output. Check Runtime › Change runtime type, then run the cell again; output never updates on its own.

NameError on a variable you definitely made. The machine was recycled. Colab disconnects notebooks that sit idle, and every runtime has a maximum lifetime (up to 12 hours on the free tier, often less). The notebook is safe in Drive, but its variables are not. Runtime › Run all rebuilds everything from the top. The next two lessons show how to save trained weights so they survive this.

A notice that you're connected to a GPU but not using it. Colab watches for GPUs sitting idle. If you're doing a small CPU-sized lesson, accept the offer to switch, or use Runtime › Disconnect and delete runtime when you finish. Either one stops spending your allowance on nothing.

💡 Tip

A good habit from day one: put import torch and the CUDA check at the top of every notebook. If the GPU silently disappears, you'll see it in the first cell instead of finding out from a slow training run.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You switch the runtime to T4 GPU and rerun torch.cuda.is_available(), which now prints True. The next cell uses a list called images that you built earlier and fails with NameError. Why?

  • Lists live in ordinary CPU memory on the machine, GPU or not. The problem is which machine you're on.

  • Saving the runtime type starts a fresh virtual machine. Rerun the cell that builds images, or use Runtime › Run all.

  • Checking for a GPU changes nothing; it only reports what the machine has.

Show answer

B. Saving the runtime type starts a fresh virtual machine. Rerun the cell that builds images, or use Runtime › Run all.

2A friend's laptop is a MacBook with an M-series chip. They install PyTorch and torch.cuda.is_available() prints False. What's going on?

  • The install is fine. A False here is the correct answer for that hardware.

  • Apple silicon uses a different backend (mps). For this course, Colab's T4 is the simpler path.

  • T4 GPU is a Colab runtime option. It isn't hardware inside the laptop.

Show answer

B. Apple silicon uses a different backend (mps). For this course, Colab's T4 is the simpler path.

#Further reading

  • Colab's FAQ (opens in a new tab): Google's own answers on usage limits, runtime lifetimes, and why free GPU access varies.
  • PyTorch: Start Locally (opens in a new tab): the install selector, if you do want PyTorch on your own computer later.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pick a device with one line that works on a Colab GPU, a Colab CPU, and your laptop.
  • Move a model and a batch with .to(device), and remember which of the two moves in place.
  • Read and fix "Expected all tensors to be on the same device".
  • Bring results back to the CPU with .item(), .detach(), and .cpu().
  • Time GPU code honestly with torch.cuda.synchronize().

You've switched on the GPU. Here is the error you're most likely to meet next, word for word as PyTorch prints it:

A GPU has its own memory, separate from the computer's main RAM. Every tensor lives in exactly one of those places, and PyTorch will not quietly copy data between them, because copying is slow and doing it by accident inside a training loop would wreck your speed without telling you. So the rule is simple: everything that meets in one operation must already be on the same device. This lesson gives you the handful of habits that make that automatic.

#One line picks the device

Start every notebook with this. Make a new cell in dlcv-setup.ipynb and run it:

This page was built on a machine without CUDA, so it prints cpu. In Colab with a T4 it prints cuda. From here on, write device everywhere instead of typing "cuda", and the same notebook runs unchanged on a GPU runtime, a CPU runtime, or your laptop.

📝 Note

Recent PyTorch versions also have torch.accelerator.current_accelerator(), which picks whatever accelerator the machine has, including Apple's mps. This course uses the explicit CUDA check because Colab's GPUs are NVIDIA ones and the explicit line is easier to read.

#Tensors: .to() hands you a copy

.to() converts a tensor to another device or dtype. For tensors it returns a new tensor and leaves the original alone. Predict what this prints before you run it:

The middle line does real work and then discards it, so x is unchanged. Moving between devices behaves the same way: x.to(device) on a line by itself leaves x on the CPU, and the device error shows up later, far from the line that caused it. Always assign: x = x.to(device).

You can also skip the copy by creating a tensor where it will be used: torch.randn(4, 3, device=device).

#Models: .to() moves the parameters in place

Modules work differently. model.to(device) moves the model's weights in place and returns the same model, so assigning is optional. Here's a small network of the kind you'll build in Module 2, moved to the device along with a batch of 16 fake inputs:

next(model.parameters()) grabs the first weight tensor, a quick way to ask where a model lives. The pattern you'll use in every training loop: move the model once, right after building it, then move each batch as it comes out of the data loader. Forget the second part and you get the error from the top of this lesson, naming cuda:0 and cpu.

The device error has a CPU twin you can trigger right here: the model's weights are float32, so a float64 batch can't meet them.

Same idea, different attribute. Two tensors in one operation must agree on device and dtype. NumPy arrays are float64 by default, so this one bites whenever you build tensors from NumPy; .float() fixes it.

#Coming back to the CPU: .item(), .detach(), .cpu()

NumPy and matplotlib can only read CPU memory, and they know nothing about gradients. That's why plotting a model's output often fails the first time:

out came from a model whose weights are tracked for gradients (you'll see why in Module 3), so PyTorch refuses to hand it to NumPy as-is. On a GPU the same call fails for a second reason too:

The full return trip is a chain, and the order is worth memorizing:

.detach() drops the gradient tracking, .cpu() copies to main memory (and does nothing if the tensor is already there), and .numpy() shares that memory with a NumPy array. For a single number, such as a loss, .item() does the whole trip and returns a plain Python float. You'll call loss.item() in every training loop in this course.

#Timing GPU code honestly

GPU calls are asynchronous: when Python reaches a @ b, it queues the work for the GPU and moves straight on. If you stop a timer right after, you measure how long it took to queue the job, not to do it. torch.cuda.synchronize() waits until the GPU has finished everything queued so far. Paste this into Colab and run it once on a CPU runtime and once on the T4:

Each row reports the time for one n × n multiplication and the speed it implies. On the T4, the speed should climb as n grows, because small matrices can't keep thousands of GPU cores busy. Write both sets of numbers down; you'll want them when you choose between CPU and GPU runs in Module 7.

🧪 Try it yourself

Delete both torch.cuda.synchronize() lines and run it again on the T4. The times collapse to almost nothing and the "TFLOP/s" column climbs past anything the hardware can actually do. That impossible number is what an unsynchronized timer looks like.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A training loop has the line xb.to(device) on its own, followed by pred = model(xb). The model was moved to cuda. What happens?

  • That's true for modules, not tensors. For a tensor, .to() returns a moved copy, and this line throws it away.

  • xb is still on the CPU while the weights are on cuda:0. Writing xb = xb.to(device) fixes it.

  • PyTorch never copies between devices behind your back; it raises an error instead.

Show answer

B. xb is still on the CPU while the weights are on cuda:0. Writing xb = xb.to(device) fixes it.

2Your timer says a 4096 × 4096 matrix multiply on the T4 took 0.03 ms, which works out to thousands of TFLOP/s. What's the most likely explanation?

  • No chip beats its own peak rating by that much. The measurement is wrong, not the hardware.

  • GPU work is queued asynchronously, so without a synchronize you timed the queueing. Synchronize before reading the clock.

  • PyTorch doesn't cache results of matrix multiplications; every call does the arithmetic again.

Show answer

B. GPU work is queued asynchronously, so without a synchronize you timed the queueing. Synchronize before reading the clock.

3You want to plot preds, a model output on the GPU. Which line works?

  • This fails twice over: preds is on the GPU and it's tracked for gradients.

  • Copying to the CPU is necessary but not enough; the tensor is still tracked for gradients, so the conversion to NumPy fails.

  • Stop tracking, copy to main memory, then convert. That's the full return trip.

Show answer

C. Stop tracking, copy to main memory, then convert. That's the full return trip.

#Further reading

  • PyTorch: CUDA semantics (opens in a new tab): the official notes on devices, asynchronous execution, and why synchronize matters.
  • PyTorch: Tensors tutorial (opens in a new tab): a short tour of creating tensors and moving them to an accelerator.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Say what survives when a Colab runtime ends and what disappears with it.
  • Save and reload a model's weights with state_dict, and keep the file in Google Drive.
  • Seed PyTorch so two runs of the same cell give the same numbers.
  • Lay out a notebook so Restart session and run all reproduces your results.
  • Debug by checking shape, dtype, and device first, then shrinking the bug to a few lines.

You start a training run, go get dinner, and come back to a notebook with a Reconnect button. Every cell is still there, the printed loss values are still there, and the trained model is gone. Forty minutes of GPU time left no trace except text.

That isn't bad luck. It's how Colab is designed, and once you know which parts are temporary, it stops costing you anything.

#What lives where

The notebook (your code, text, and the last outputs) autosaves to Drive. The machine running it is rented, and when the runtime ends, Colab throws the whole machine away: variables, trained models, downloaded datasets, and files you wrote to /content. The fix is to write anything you'd hate to lose to a path inside Google Drive.

#Save weights, not just code

A trained model is its architecture plus its numbers. The architecture is already in your code, so what you save is the numbers. Every PyTorch module has a state dict: an ordered dictionary from each parameter's name to its tensor.

The names come from the positions in nn.Sequential: layer 0 is the first Linear, layer 1 is the ReLU (no weights, so it's missing), and layer 2 is the second Linear. Saving and loading is two lines each way:

fresh starts with different random weights, then load_state_dict overwrites every one of them, so both models now give identical outputs. Notice that you have to build fresh with the same layers first; the file holds numbers, not code. weights_only=True tells torch.load to accept only tensors and plain containers, which is what a state dict is, and refuse anything that could run code.

In Colab, mount your Drive once per session and save there instead. Colab asks for permission the first time:

Weights saved from a GPU remember they were on cuda. To load them on a machine without a GPU, add map_location="cpu" to torch.load.

#Same seed, same numbers

Neural networks are full of randomness: starting weights, the order batches are shuffled in, dropout. That's fine for learning and terrible for debugging, because you can't tell whether an edit helped or the dice just rolled differently. Setting a seed makes the random sequence repeat:

The first two lines match because each starts from seed 42. The third differs, since it continues the sequence instead of restarting it. So the seed has to be set before the model is built, and the cells after it have to run in the same order every time.

PyTorch, NumPy, and Python's random module each keep their own generator, and scikit-learn uses random_state arguments. On a GPU, a few operations aren't bit-for-bit repeatable even with seeds, so tiny differences in the fourth decimal place between runs are normal there. Differences in the first decimal place mean something in your code changed.

#A notebook layout that survives a restart

Notebooks let you run cells in any order, which is how a notebook ends up "working" only because of a cell you since deleted. Two habits prevent that. First, every notebook in this course starts with one setup cell:

Imports, seeds, the device, and every number you might tune live in one place, so a change to the learning rate is a change to one line. Second, before you trust or share a result, use Runtime › Restart session and run all (some older guides call it Restart runtime). If the notebook still produces the same numbers from a cold start, the result is real.

Name notebooks after the lesson (m4-l2-digits.ipynb), keep them in one Drive folder, and use File › Save a copy in Drive whenever you open someone else's notebook, so your edits are saved to a copy you own.

#Debugging: shape, dtype, device

Most PyTorch errors are about one of three properties of a tensor: its shape, its dtype, or its device. When a line fails, print those three for every tensor on that line before you change anything. This helper does it in one call, and you'll reuse it all course:

Read the dtype column. Classification losses in PyTorch expect class labels as whole numbers (int64), and these are float32. Here's the crash that mismatch causes, reproduced in three lines with nothing but random tensors:

That's the second habit: shrink the bug. Rebuild the failing line in a fresh cell using torch.randn with the same shapes and dtypes. If the small version fails the same way, you've found the cause without your data, your model, or your other 40 cells in the way, and the fix (here, labels.long()) takes seconds. If the small version works, the difference between it and your real code is where the bug lives.

When you ask someone for help, whether that's a forum like discuss.pytorch.org or a friend, send the small version, the full error message, and the output of torch.__version__ and device. A three-line reproduction usually gets an answer in minutes; a whole notebook often gets none.

#How the rest of the course works

Modules 2 to 7 each have three lessons: Notes that teach the ideas with code you can run, a Build-along that uses them to make one complete thing, and Practice with exercises, hints, and worked solutions. Type the code into your own notebook rather than copying it. Every output on these pages came from really running the code, so if your numbers differ, that's a clue worth chasing, not a typo in the lesson.

⚠️ Watch out

Saving with torch.save(model, path) (the whole model, not its state_dict()) also works, but it pickles the model's Python class. Rename a file or edit the class later and the checkpoint can stop loading. Save the state dict, and keep the architecture in code.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You saved model.state_dict() to Drive yesterday. Today, in a new session, you run model.load_state_dict(torch.load(path, weights_only=True)) as the first line and get NameError: name 'model' is not defined. What's missing?

  • Files in Drive stay until you delete them. The error names model, not the file.

  • Run the cell that defines the layers, then load the weights into it.

  • Seeds matter when weights are random. Loading replaces every weight, so the seed is irrelevant here.

Show answer

B. Run the cell that defines the layers, then load the weights into it.

2Two runs of the same notebook give accuracies of 0.912 and 0.874. You set torch.manual_seed(0) in the setup cell. Which is the most likely cause?

  • That causes differences in the fourth decimal place or so, not four percentage points.

  • The seed fixes the sequence from that point on. Restart the session and run all cells from the top to compare fairly.

  • Zero is an ordinary seed value. It fixes the sequence; it doesn't remove the randomness.

Show answer

B. The seed fixes the sequence from that point on. Restart the session and run all cells from the top to compare fairly.

Key takeaways

  • Colab keeps your notebook and throws away the machine. Save weights to a Google Drive path with torch.save(model.state_dict(), path).
  • Loading needs the same architecture built first: model.load_state_dict(torch.load(path, weights_only=True)).
  • Seed before you build anything, and confirm results with Restart session and run all.
  • For any error, check shape, dtype, and device, then shrink the failing line to a few lines of torch.randn.

#Further reading

  • PyTorch: Saving and loading models (opens in a new tab): state dicts, checkpoints that also store the optimizer, and loading across devices.
  • PyTorch: Reproducibility (opens in a new tab): which sources of randomness exist and how far seeding can take you on a GPU.
  • Andrej Karpathy: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks (opens in a new tab): a practitioner's checklist for catching silent bugs; you'll use several of its tricks in Module 4.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read a tensor's shape, dtype, and device, and explain the (N, C, H, W) image convention.
  • Reshape, flatten, and permute tensors, and tell a legal reshape from a correct one.
  • Predict the result shape of a broadcast, or the error it raises.
  • Write nn.Linear as a matrix multiply and count its parameters.
  • Compare ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh, and spot where each one saturates.

Here are 32 handwritten digits from scikit-learn, each an 8 × 8 grid of pixel brightnesses. A dense layer that takes 64 inputs should be a perfect fit, since 8 × 8 = 64. Let's load them and find out.

Now hand the batch to the layer:

The numbers in the message are the whole story. nn.Linear only looks at the last dimension of its input and treats every dimension before it as a pile of separate rows. Our batch has shape (32, 1, 8, 8), so the layer saw 32 × 1 × 8 = 256 rows of 8 numbers each, and an 8-number row can't meet a layer that wants 64. The digits were never wrong; the shape was. Most bugs in this course look like this one, so this lesson is about reading shapes fluently.

#Shape, dtype, device: three facts about every tensor

A tensor is an n-dimensional grid of numbers that all share one type. Three attributes tell you nearly everything about it:

Image batches in PyTorch follow the (N, C, H, W) convention: batch size, channels, height, width. The digits are grayscale, so C is 1; a color photo batch would be (N, 3, H, W). That's why we called .unsqueeze(1), which inserts a new dimension of size 1 at position 1, turning (32, 8, 8) into (32, 1, 8, 8).

The last line shows a trap. NumPy defaults to float64, and so does a tensor built from a NumPy array unless you say otherwise. PyTorch layers are float32, and as you saw last module, mixing the two raises an error. Labels are the opposite case: they should be int64 whole numbers, and they are.

#Reshaping: legal is not the same as correct

flatten(start_dim=1) squashes everything after the batch dimension into one, giving each image a row of 64 pixels. That fixes the opening bug:

The -1 in reshape means "work this dimension out for me." reshape(64, -1) is perfectly legal (2,048 numbers fit into 64 rows of 32) and a disaster: each new row mixes pixels from different images. Reshaping keeps the numbers in their memory order and only redraws the row boundaries. Reordering dimensions is a different operation, permute (or .T for a 2-D tensor). The difference shows up clearly on a tiny example:

Both results have shape (3, 2), but only the transpose moves 3 under 0. You'll need permute in Module 5, when images loaded as (H, W, C) must become (C, H, W).

#Broadcasting: how shapes that differ still combine

You often combine tensors of different shapes: adding a bias of shape (10,) to outputs of shape (32, 10), or subtracting a per-pixel mean. PyTorch broadcasts: it lines the shapes up from the right and compares one dimension at a time. Two sizes are compatible if they're equal or if one of them is 1 (a missing dimension counts as 1). A size-1 dimension is stretched to match, without copying any data. Step through the rule written out in plain Python:

The second call is the classic bug. Say you want to center each image by subtracting its own average brightness. flat.mean(dim=1) gives one number per image, shape (32,), and broadcasting lines that 32 up against the 64 pixel columns:

keepdim=True keeps the averaged dimension as size 1, giving shape (32, 1), which broadcasts across the columns the way you meant:

The row means print as zero, or as tiny numbers like 1e-8 from rounding. The dangerous case is a mistake that broadcasts without an error, such as (32, 1) meeting (32,), which silently produces a (32, 32) grid. When a result has a shape you didn't expect, check the broadcast first.

#nn.Linear is a matrix multiply plus a bias

Matrix multiplication with @ follows one shape rule: (N, k) @ (k, M) gives (N, M), and the inner sizes must match. A dense (fully connected) layer is exactly that. nn.Linear(64, 10) stores a weight matrix W of shape (10, 64), one row per output, and a bias b of shape (10,), and computes y = x @ W.T + b:

Each of the 10 outputs is a weighted sum of all 64 pixels plus its own bias, so the layer has 64 × 10 + 10 = 650 parameters. The bias add is a broadcast: (32, 10) + (10,).

Now the reason layers need anything else. Stack two linear layers with nothing between them, and the pair collapses into a single linear layer: W2(W1 x + b1) + b2 = (W2 W1) x + (W2 b1 + b2). Here's that algebra checked numerically:

A hundred stacked linear layers can only draw straight boundaries, the same as one. Depth only buys you something if a nonlinear function sits between the layers.

#Activations bend the line, and sometimes flatten it

An activation function is applied to every number a layer outputs. The three classics:

  • ReLU: max(0, z). Passes positive values through and zeroes out the rest. The default choice for hidden layers.
  • Sigmoid: 1 / (1 + e^(-z)). Squeezes any number into (0, 1). Used for probabilities in yes/no outputs.
  • tanh: squeezes into (-1, 1), centered on zero.

The right half of this chart shows each function's slope. In Module 3 you'll see that learning sends its signal backward through these slopes, so a slope near zero means almost no learning signal gets through.

Here are the exact numbers for a few inputs. Predict the sigmoid slope at z = 10 before you look:

At z = 10 the sigmoid outputs 0.99995 and its slope is about 0.00005, roughly 5,000 times smaller than at zero. A unit sitting out there is saturated: nudging its weights barely changes its output, so it learns almost nothing. That happens easily when inputs are large, which is one reason you'll scale pixels from 0–16 down to 0–1 in the next lesson. ReLU never saturates for positive inputs, but a unit whose input is negative for every example outputs zero with zero slope, a dead unit.

#Mistakes that cost an afternoon

⚠️ Watch out

Flattening away the batch. x.reshape(-1) or x.view(-1) turns a (32, 1, 8, 8) batch into one row of 2,048 numbers. Use x.flatten(start_dim=1) or nn.Flatten(), which both keep dimension 0, so every image stays its own row.

  • float64 from NumPy. torch.tensor(array) copies NumPy's dtype. Add dtype=torch.float32 or call .float().
  • Forgetting keepdim=True. A reduction such as mean(dim=1) deletes that dimension, and the broadcast that follows either fails or, worse, quietly builds a grid.
  • reshape where you meant permute. If you're reordering axes, the result must move data, and reshape never does.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A batch has shape (16, 64) and goes through nn.Linear(64, 32). What's the output shape, and how many parameters does the layer have?

  • The layer maps 64 features to 32, so the last dimension changes. And the bias adds parameters on top of the 64 × 32 weights.

  • The batch size passes through untouched. Weights are 32 × 64 = 2,048, plus 32 biases.

  • Linear never changes the batch dimension; it only transforms the last one.

Show answer

B. The batch size passes through untouched. Weights are 32 × 64 = 2,048, plus 32 biases.

2What shape does torch.zeros(32, 1) + torch.zeros(10) produce?

  • A size of 1 is always compatible: it stretches to match the other size.

  • Broadcasting stretches the size-1 dimension rather than shrinking the other tensor.

  • Aligned from the right: 1 against 10 gives 10, then 32 against a missing dimension gives 32.

Show answer

C. Aligned from the right: 1 against 10 gives 10, then 32 against a missing dimension gives 32.

3Two nn.Linear layers are stacked with no activation between them. Compared with a single nn.Linear, what can the pair represent?

  • The weights multiply into one matrix and the biases into one vector, as the allclose check showed. Only a nonlinearity between them adds power.

  • Parameter count isn't what matters. The function is still linear, so boundaries stay straight.

  • The output size is set by the last layer, not by how many layers there are.

Show answer

A. The weights multiply into one matrix and the biases into one vector, as the allclose check showed. Only a nonlinearity between them adds power.

4A hidden layer uses sigmoid, and most of its pre-activation values are around 8 or larger. What will you observe during training?

  • Outputs near 1 mean the curve is flat there, which is the opposite of fast learning.

  • The slope at z = 8 is about 0.0003, so the learning signal flowing back through those units almost vanishes.

  • Sigmoid accepts any real number. That's exactly why it can be pushed into its flat regions.

Show answer

B. The slope at z = 8 is about 0.0003, so the learning signal flowing back through those units almost vanishes.

Key takeaways

  • Every tensor has a shape, a dtype, and a device; print all three before you guess at a bug.
  • nn.Linear acts on the last dimension only: (..., in) becomes (..., out), computed as x @ W.T + b.
  • Keep the batch dimension when flattening: flatten(start_dim=1), never reshape(-1).
  • Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right; sizes must match or be 1. Use keepdim=True after reductions.
  • Without activations, stacked linear layers collapse into one. Sigmoid and tanh saturate for large inputs; ReLU units can die.

#Further reading

  • PyTorch: Broadcasting semantics (opens in a new tab): the official rules, including in-place operations, where broadcasting is stricter.
  • PyTorch: nn.Linear (opens in a new tab): the exact formula, weight shapes, and how the weights are initialized.
  • CS231n: Neural Networks Part 1 (opens in a new tab): Stanford's notes on activation functions, including a clear section on dying ReLUs and saturated sigmoids.

What you'll learn

  • Turn NumPy images into a correctly shaped, scaled float32 batch.
  • Build a multilayer perceptron with nn.Sequential and count its parameters.
  • Follow a batch through every layer and explain each shape change, from pixels to class probabilities.
  • Write shape_report, a tracer built on forward hooks that prints shapes, parameters, and activation health for any nn.Sequential.
  • Use the tracer to find a saturated sigmoid layer caused by unscaled inputs, and fix it.

By the end of this build you'll have two things: a small network that turns an 8 × 8 handwritten digit into ten class probabilities, and a tool called shape_report that X-rays any nn.Sequential model. The tool prints every layer's output shape and parameter count and flags layers whose activations have gone flat. You'll use it to catch a bug that raises no error at all.

Here's the network we're building, with the shape of a 16-image batch at every stage:

Make a new Colab notebook called m2-l2-tracer.ipynb and put each step in its own cell.

#Step 1: look at the data

scikit-learn ships 1,797 handwritten digits, each scanned at 8 × 8 pixels with brightness from 0 to 16. They come with the library, so nothing downloads.

The shape (1797, 8, 8) means 1,797 images of 8 rows by 8 columns. The images are tiny, which is exactly why they're good for tracing: every number we print is something you can reason about.

#Step 2: make a batch PyTorch can use

A batch needs three things fixed: dtype (float32), shape ((N, C, H, W)), and scale. Pixels from 0 to 16 become 0 to 1 by dividing by 16.

unsqueeze(1) adds the channel dimension, and y holds int64 class labels, the type classification losses expect. Why bother scaling? Hold that question; Step 6 answers it with evidence.

#Step 3: build the network and count its weights

nn.Sequential runs its layers in order, feeding each one's output to the next. nn.Flatten() comes first, so the model accepts image-shaped batches directly.

Check the count by hand: (64 × 32 + 32) + (32 × 10 + 10) = 2,080 + 330 = 2,410. The (0) to (3) on the left are the layer indexes, which become the names in the model's state dict.

#Step 4: walk the batch through, one layer at a time

nn.Sequential is iterable, so you can run its layers yourself and print what comes out of each:

The final layer's outputs are logits: ten raw scores per image, any real number. softmax turns each row into probabilities by exponentiating and dividing by the row's total, so every row sums to 1 (up to rounding). argmax(dim=1) picks the highest-probability class per image.

The predictions are nonsense, and they should be: the weights are random. Training (Module 4) is the process that makes these match the true labels.

⚠️ Watch out

torch.softmax(logits, dim=0) runs without complaint and gives the wrong answer: it normalizes each column across the 16 images instead of each image across its 10 classes. Rows then don't sum to 1. For (N, classes) tensors, the class dimension is dim=1.

#Step 5: automate the trace with forward hooks

Printing inside a loop works for nn.Sequential, but real models have custom forward methods you don't want to edit. PyTorch lets you attach a forward hook to any module: a function that runs every time that module produces an output, receiving (module, inputs, output). A hook can look without changing anything.

The tracer also measures activation health. For each activation layer it computes the slope of the activation at every output (you derived these slopes in the Notes) and reports the share that are flat, with slope below 0.01. It also counts dead units: hidden units that are flat for every example in the batch.

Three details matter. torch.no_grad() skips the bookkeeping PyTorch normally does for training, since we're only looking. handle.remove() detaches the hooks, so calling the model later doesn't keep printing. And the report works for any nn.Sequential, whatever its layers.

Read the ReLU row: about half its outputs are flat. That's healthy. ReLU zeroes every negative input by design, and with random weights roughly half the inputs are negative. The number to worry about is the dead column, units that are zero for every single image, and it says 4.

Before you panic, ask how much evidence 16 images is. A unit that happens to stay silent for these 16 digits might fire for a different 3 or 7. Run the same report on all 1,797 images:

No dead units. The four were an artifact of a small batch, which is the general lesson for every activation statistic: measure on enough data to mean something, a few hundred examples at least.

#Step 6: catch a saturated layer

Now the bug. A teammate swaps ReLU for sigmoid and, to "keep the data raw," skips the divide-by-16. Nothing crashes. Predict what the sigmoid row will show, then run the tracer on 256 raw images and on the same images scaled:

With raw pixels, the first Linear layer's outputs have a standard deviation of about 4.6, so a large share of them land where the sigmoid is flat. About a third of all sigmoid outputs carry almost no learning signal. Scaling the input shrinks that spread about sixteenfold, and the flat share drops to zero. The histograms show why:

The dashed lines sit at ±4.6, where the sigmoid's slope falls below 0.01. Everything outside them is a value that training can barely move. This is the "saturated activation stops useful change" failure, and you caught it before spending a minute on training.

#The finished program

Here is the whole build as one script you can paste into a fresh Colab cell:

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the tracer attach hooks instead of adding print calls inside the model?

  • Hooks add a little work; they never speed anything up.

  • That's what lets one shape_report work on any nn.Sequential, and later on models you didn't write.

  • It works fine. It just means editing the model and remembering to delete the prints later.

Show answer

B. That's what lets one shape_report work on any nn.Sequential, and later on models you didn't write.

2The ReLU row reports about 50% flat outputs. Is the layer broken?

  • A unit that's zero for some images still learns from the rest. One that's zero for every image never does.

  • Flat for some inputs is normal for ReLU. Only units flat for all inputs are dead, and on the full dataset the report shows none.

  • The ReLU model was given scaled inputs. ReLU's flat half comes from its shape, not from scale.

Show answer

A. A unit that's zero for some images still learns from the rest. One that's zero for every image never does.

3The raw-pixel batch makes about a third of the sigmoid outputs flat. Which fix addresses the cause?

  • That would break the probabilities and does nothing for the hidden layer.

  • More units get pushed into the same flat zones, because the inputs are still too large.

  • The report showed the flat share dropping to zero with the same weights once the inputs were divided by 16.

Show answer

C. The report showed the flat share dropping to zero with the same weights once the inputs were divided by 16.

Key takeaways

  • Fix a batch's dtype, shape, and scale before it meets the model: float32, (N, C, H, W), roughly 0 to 1.
  • nn.Sequential is iterable, and forward hooks let you watch any module's output without editing the model.
  • Logits are raw scores; softmax(dim=1) turns each row into probabilities, and argmax(dim=1) picks the class.
  • A health check on activations (flat share, dead units) catches saturation from unscaled inputs before training starts.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a column for the fraction of exact zeros in each layer's output, and compare ReLU with nn.LeakyReLU().
  • Make shape_report walk nested models with model.named_modules(), printing names like features.0 instead of class names.
  • Stack four Linear + Tanh pairs and watch the std column shrink or grow with depth as you multiply the first layer's weights by 0.5 or 2.

#Further reading

  • PyTorch: Build the Neural Network (opens in a new tab): the official walkthrough of nn.Module, nn.Sequential, nn.Flatten, and softmax on a model like this one.
  • PyTorch: register_forward_hook (opens in a new tab): the hook signature and options such as with_kwargs.

What you'll learn

  • Predict tensor shapes from broadcasting, matrix multiplication, and reductions before running code.
  • Fix shape bugs that only appear for some batch sizes.
  • Count a network's parameters by hand and confirm the count in code.
  • Standardize features without creating NaNs, and convert channels-last images correctly.
  • Measure dead and saturated units, and design a network that avoids them.

Each exercise is a few lines of PyTorch. Write your answer in a Colab cell before opening the solution, and when your output differs from the sample, figure out why before moving on. That gap is where the learning is.

#Warm-up: shapes in your head

Predict the shape of each result, then check with the cell below.

  1. torch.zeros(8, 3, 32, 32).flatten(1)
  2. torch.zeros(5, 4) @ torch.zeros(4, 7)
  3. torch.zeros(6, 1, 5) + torch.zeros(4, 1)
  4. torch.zeros(10, 64).mean(dim=0, keepdim=True)
  5. torch.zeros(10, 64).sum(dim=1)

The third is the one people miss. Aligned from the right, (6, 1, 5) and (4, 1) compare 5 with 1, then 1 with 4, then 6 with nothing, giving (6, 4, 5). Both tensors were stretched along a different dimension.

#Exercise 1: the batch that crashes on the last step

A classmate's scoring function works on every test batch of 64 digits, then crashes on the final batch of the epoch, which has only 37 images (1,797 isn't a multiple of 64). Find the bug and fix it so any batch size works.

Sample output after the fix:

Need a hint?

With 64 images, reshape(64, -1) happens to produce the right shape. Work out what it produces for 37 images: 37 × 64 numbers split into 64 rows.

Show solution

The code hard-codes the batch size in the wrong position. With 37 images, reshape(64, -1) makes 64 rows of 37 numbers, which can't meet a 64-input layer. Keep dimension 0 as the batch and flatten the rest:

A bug that depends on batch size hides until the last, smaller batch of an epoch. Test shape-sensitive code with an odd batch size like 37 on purpose.

#Exercise 2: count before you build

Count, by hand, the parameters in a network with layers 64 → 128 → 64 → 10 (ReLU between the Linear layers). Then build it and confirm, printing the size of each parameter tensor and the total.

Need a hint?

Each nn.Linear(a, b) has a × b weights and b biases. ReLU has none.

Show solution

By hand: (64 × 128 + 128) + (128 × 64 + 64) + (64 × 10 + 10) = 8,320 + 8,256 + 650 = 17,226.

model.parameters() yields weights and biases in layer order, so the list alternates weight, bias. Notice where the parameters live: the first two layers hold 96% of them. Widening an early layer is far more expensive than widening the last one.

#Exercise 3: nn.Linear by hand, for any number of leading dimensions

Write my_linear(x, W, b) using @ so that it matches nn.Linear for inputs of shape (2, 5, 64), not just (N, 64). Print the output shape and whether it matches.

Need a hint?

@ broadcasts every dimension except the last two, just like + broadcasts. Try the simplest formula first.

Show solution

The two-dimensional formula already works:

(2, 5, 64) @ (64, 3) treats the leading (2, 5) as a batch of batches and gives (2, 5, 3). The bias (3,) broadcasts across both leading dimensions. That's why nn.Linear accepts any shape ending in its input size, which is also how the opening bug in the Notes (256 rows of 8) came about.

#Exercise 4: standardize without NaNs

Standardize every pixel column of the full digits data, X = torch.tensor(load_digits().data, dtype=torch.float32), to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The obvious one-liner fills the result with nan. Find out how many NaNs it makes and which columns cause them, then fix it so there are none.

Need a hint?

Some pixels sit at the very edge of the 8 × 8 grid. What is the standard deviation of a column that's 0 for every image, and what is 0 / 0?

Show solution

Three border pixels are blank in all 1,797 images, so their standard deviation is 0 and (0 - 0) / 0 is nan. Clamp the denominator:

dim=0 reduces down the rows, giving one mean and one standard deviation per pixel column, shape (64,), which broadcasts back across the (1797, 64) data. A single NaN in an input spreads through every layer it touches and turns the loss into nan, so this check belongs in every data pipeline.

#Exercise 5: channels-last to channels-first

Images loaded with NumPy or PIL usually arrive as (N, H, W, C), but PyTorch's image layers expect (N, C, H, W). Build a fake batch where every red value is 1, every green is 2, and every blue is 3, convert it, and prove that channel 0 now contains only red values. Also show what reshape does instead.

Need a hint?

Name the target position of each old dimension. Old order: N=0, H=1, W=2, C=3. New order: N, C, H, W.

Show solution

permute(0, 3, 1, 2) reads as "new dim 0 is old 0, new dim 1 is old 3 (C), then old 1 (H) and old 2 (W)". reshape produces the same shape but keeps the memory order, where red, green, and blue alternate pixel by pixel, so each "channel" ends up a mixture of all three colors. A model trained on that still runs, and quietly learns from scrambled pixels.

#Exercise 6: count the dead units

Write dead_units(linear, x), which applies a Linear layer and then ReLU to the inputs x and returns how many of the layer's units output zero for every row. Test it on nn.Linear(64, 32) with the full scaled digits (load_digits().data / 16), first as initialized, then after simulating a bad update that lowered every bias by 0.5.

Need a hint?

After ReLU, h has shape (1797, 32). A unit is a column. (h == 0) is a boolean grid; which reduction asks "true in every row of this column"?

Show solution

.all(dim=0) collapses the rows and leaves one True or False per unit. Lowering the biases by just 0.5 pushes 20 of 32 units below zero for every digit. A dead unit's slope is 0 for every input, so no training signal ever reaches its weights, and it can't recover by itself. Large learning rates cause exactly this kind of jump, which is one reason Module 4 watches them closely.

#Challenge: a network that passes the spec

Your network will receive color images of shape (N, 3, 8, 8) with raw pixel values from 0 to 255, exactly as a camera produces them, and must output 5 class scores. The spec:

  • output shape (N, 5);
  • at most 10,000 parameters, with at least two hidden layers using nn.Tanh;
  • on torch.rand(512, 3, 8, 8) * 255, no tanh layer may have more than 5% of its outputs flat (slope below 0.01);
  • scaling must happen inside the model, because the people calling it will send raw pixels.

Write a check that prints the output shape, the parameter count, and each tanh layer's flat share.

Need a hint?

nn.Sequential has no layer that divides by a constant, so write one: a class that subclasses nn.Module, calls super().__init__(), and returns x * self.factor from forward. Run the check without it first to see why the spec demands it.

Show solution

Parameters: (192 × 40 + 40) + (40 × 24 + 24) + (24 × 5 + 5) = 7,720 + 984 + 125 = 8,829. Scale has no parameters, so it's free. Without it, about 97% of the first tanh layer's outputs are pinned at ±1. The second layer looks healthy only because its inputs are already squashed into −1 to 1, so a per-layer check matters: an average over the whole network would have hidden the problem. With scaling built in, both layers are 0% flat, and callers can't forget it.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Compute mean squared error and cross-entropy by hand, and say which one a task needs.
  • Explain why cross-entropy keeps learning when a sigmoid output is confidently wrong.
  • Derive the gradient of a one-neuron model with the chain rule, then confirm it with loss.backward().
  • Describe gradient descent as steps on a loss surface, and predict when a learning rate makes the loss explode.

A model has one weight, w, and predicts y = w · x. The data is four points that lie exactly on y = 2x, so the best weight is 2. Start at w = 0, compute which way is downhill, step that way, and repeat. Step through it and watch the loss column:

Every step moves w in the downhill direction, exactly as designed, and the loss goes 30, 120, 480. The direction is right and the scale is wrong: each step jumps clear over the valley and lands higher up the far side. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to calculate the learning rate where that starts. First, the pieces: what the loss measures, what the gradient is, and how PyTorch computes it.

#A loss turns "how wrong" into one number

Training needs a single number to push down. A loss function compares predictions with the truth and returns it.

For predicting quantities (a price, an angle, a box coordinate), the standard choice is mean squared error: the average of (prediction − truth)². Squaring makes every miss positive and punishes big misses much more than small ones.

For classification, the model outputs a probability for each class, and cross-entropy looks only at the probability given to the right one: the loss is −log(p_true). A confident correct answer (p_true near 1) costs almost nothing; a confident wrong one (p_true near 0) costs a lot. In PyTorch you hand F.cross_entropy the raw logits; it applies softmax itself.

The model gives class 0 a probability of 0.7856, so the loss is −log(0.7856) = 0.2413, and PyTorch agrees. Plot the loss against p_true for both choices and the difference is obvious:

Squared error caps out at 1, so a model that's 99% sure of the wrong class is charged about the same as one that's 60% sure. Cross-entropy keeps climbing. There's a second, bigger reason to prefer it for classifiers, and it shows up in the gradients below.

#The gradient of one neuron, by hand

Take one neuron with no activation: ŷ = w·x + b, with squared error L = (ŷ − y)². Use concrete numbers: x = 2, y = 7, w = 1, b = 0.5. The forward pass gives ŷ = 2.5, an error of e = ŷ − y = −4.5, and a loss of 20.25.

The gradient answers: if I nudge w up by a tiny amount, how much does L change, and in which direction? The loss depends on w only through a chain of steps, w → ŷ → e → L, and the chain rule says to multiply the local rate of change at each link:

  • dL/de = 2e = −9
  • de/dŷ = 1
  • dŷ/dw = x = 2, and dŷ/db = 1

So dL/dw = 2e · 1 · x = −18 and dL/db = 2e · 1 · 1 = −9. The negative sign says increasing w would lower the loss; the size says the loss is about 18 times as sensitive as the change in w, for small changes. Notice that dL/de = −9 was computed once and reused for both weights. That reuse is backpropagation: one pass backward from the loss, handing each link the gradient from the link after it, gives the gradient for every parameter at the cost of roughly one extra forward pass.

#Autograd checks your calculus

PyTorch does that backward pass for you. Mark the tensors you want gradients for with requires_grad=True, compute the loss, call .backward(), and read .grad:

−18 and −9, matching the hand calculation. As PyTorch runs the forward pass it records every operation in a graph like the diagram above, and .backward() walks it in reverse.

Now the promised reason for cross-entropy. Take a sigmoid neuron whose logit is z = −6 for an example whose true label is 1. It outputs p = 0.0025: confidently wrong. Compare the gradient each loss sends back to z:

With squared error, the chain passes through the sigmoid's slope, which at z = −6 is about 0.0025, so the neuron that most needs correcting gets a gradient near zero: the saturation problem from Module 2. With cross-entropy, the sigmoid's slope cancels out of the algebra and the gradient is simply p − y = −0.9975. Being confidently wrong produces the largest possible push, not the smallest.

⚠️ Watch out

Gradients add up. .backward() adds into .grad; it doesn't overwrite. Run the forward pass and backward() a second time without clearing, and w.grad becomes −36. Every training loop clears gradients before each backward pass, with optimizer.zero_grad(), as you'll see in the next lesson.

#Gradient descent: walking down a loss surface

With two parameters, the loss is a surface over the (w, b) plane, and the gradient points uphill. Gradient descent repeats one update, w ← w − lr · dL/dw (and the same for b), where the learning rate lr sets the step size. Here it is on 20 noisy points around the line y = 3x − 1, starting from (w, b) = (−1, 2) with three learning rates:

The valley is a stretched bowl: the loss is far more sensitive to b than to w here, because the x values are small. A learning rate of 0.05 heads in the right direction but needs hundreds of steps. At 0.3 the path curves smoothly toward the bottom. At 0.85 each step overshoots in the steep b direction, so the path bounces from wall to wall, with each bounce a little smaller, while it moves along w.

#How large is too large?

Go back to the opening trace. For that loss, each update multiplies the distance from the best weight, w − 2, by the same factor, 1 − lr · 15, where 15 is the loss's curvature (its second derivative, 2 · mean(x²)). With lr = 0.2 the factor is −2: every step flips to the other side and doubles the distance, so the loss, which grows with the distance squared, quadruples. The rule that falls out: descent converges only when lr is below 2 / curvature, here 2/15 ≈ 0.133. In the steepest direction of the surface above, the curvature is about 2, so the limit is just under 1.0. A learning rate of 0.85 bounces but survives; 1.05 does not:

Look closely at 0.85: despite all that bouncing, it reaches the bottom sooner than 0.3. Big steps overshoot in the steep direction but make fast progress along the shallow one, so the quickest learning rates usually sit just below the edge, and one step past it the loss explodes.

Real networks have millions of directions with different curvatures, so you can't compute the limit by hand. But the symptoms are the same, and you'll learn to read them from loss curves in Module 4: too small crawls, too large bounces or blows up to inf and then nan.

#Mistakes worth recognizing

  • Applying softmax before F.cross_entropy. It expects logits and applies its own log-softmax, so you'd squash the probabilities twice. The loss still decreases, slowly, and never gets near zero.
  • Float labels for classification. F.cross_entropy wants class indices as int64 with shape (N,), not floats.
  • Reading a single gradient as the whole story. A gradient is a local slope. It tells you the best direction for a tiny step, not how far to go. That's the learning rate's job.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model gives the true class a probability of 0.05. What is its cross-entropy loss for that example?

  • That's the probability itself. The loss is the negative log of it.

  • −log(0.05) ≈ 3.0. A confident mistake costs far more than the 0.9 squared error would charge.

  • That's 1 − p. Cross-entropy is −log p, which grows without limit as p approaches 0.

Show answer

B. −log(0.05) ≈ 3.0. A confident mistake costs far more than the 0.9 squared error would charge.

2For ŷ = w·x + b and L = (ŷ − y)², with x = 3, y = 1, w = 1, and b = 0, what is dL/dw?

  • That's 2e, which is dL/db. For w you multiply by one more link, dŷ/dw = x = 3.

  • ŷ = 3, e = 2, so dL/dw = 2e · x = 2 · 2 · 3 = 12.

  • Close, but the derivative of e² is 2e, so the factor of 2 belongs in front.

Show answer

B. ŷ = 3, e = 2, so dL/dw = 2e · x = 2 · 2 · 3 = 12.

3You call loss.backward() in a loop without ever clearing .grad. What goes wrong?

  • .backward() adds into .grad, so old gradients stay in the total.

  • The accumulated sum mixes every past gradient. Clear with optimizer.zero_grad() before each backward pass.

  • It raises an error only if you reuse the same graph twice. A fresh forward pass followed by backward() runs fine and silently accumulates.

Show answer

B. The accumulated sum mixes every past gradient. Clear with optimizer.zero_grad() before each backward pass.

4For a loss whose curvature in its steepest direction is 50, which learning rate makes gradient descent diverge?

  • 0.01 × 50 = 0.5, so the factor is 1 − 0.5 = 0.5: safely shrinking.

  • 1 − 0.03 × 50 = −0.5: it overshoots each time but the distance still halves, so it converges.

  • The limit is 2 / 50 = 0.04. At 0.05 the factor is 1 − 2.5 = −1.5, so each step lands farther away than the last.

Show answer

C. The limit is 2 / 50 = 0.04. At 0.05 the factor is 1 − 2.5 = −1.5, so each step lands farther away than the last.

Key takeaways

  • Use mean squared error for quantities and cross-entropy (on logits) for classes; cross-entropy keeps a strong gradient when the model is confidently wrong.
  • The chain rule multiplies local slopes from the loss back to each weight; backpropagation reuses the shared links so every gradient costs one backward pass.
  • loss.backward() fills .grad for every tensor with requires_grad=True, and it adds, so gradients must be cleared each step.
  • Gradient descent steps against the gradient. Too small a learning rate crawls; above 2 / curvature the loss grows every step.

#Further reading

  • PyTorch: Automatic differentiation with torch.autograd (opens in a new tab): computational graphs, requires_grad, and turning tracking off.
  • CS231n: Backpropagation, intuitions (opens in a new tab): Stanford's notes on the chain rule as local gradients flowing through circuit diagrams.
  • Distill: Why Momentum Really Works (opens in a new tab): interactive diagrams of gradient descent on stretched valleys like the one above, and the fix that most optimizers build on.

What you'll learn

  • Write a sigmoid neuron's forward pass and binary cross-entropy loss with plain tensor operations.
  • Derive its gradient, Xᵀ(p − y) / N, and verify it two independent ways.
  • Train it with a hand-written update loop and draw the path it takes across the loss surface.
  • Run a learning-rate sweep and read the crawl, the sweet spot, and the cliff.
  • Replace the hand-written update with torch.optim.SGD and get identical weights.

In the Notes you computed one gradient for one example. Now you'll do it for a whole dataset, the way a real training loop does, and you won't trust your own math until two independent checks agree with it. The model is the smallest real classifier there is: one neuron with a sigmoid, separating two clouds of points. It has only two weights, so you can draw its entire loss surface and watch training walk across it.

#Step 1: two clouds of points

make_blobs draws points around two centers. They overlap a little, so no straight line can separate them perfectly, which keeps the best possible loss above zero.

Labels are float32 this time, because binary cross-entropy compares them directly with probabilities.

#Step 2: forward pass and loss, by hand

The neuron computes a score z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ for each point (no bias, to keep exactly two weights), turns it into a probability p = sigmoid(z), and is charged the binary cross-entropy: −log p when the label is 1 and −log(1 − p) when it's 0, averaged over all points. We start from a deliberately bad guess, w = (−2, 2.5).

Both say 1.6713. In real code, prefer binary_cross_entropy_with_logits: it takes the score z and combines the sigmoid and the log in a way that can't produce log(0) when p rounds to exactly 0 or 1.

#Step 3: derive the gradient

Follow one point i back from the loss to the weights, the same chain as in the Notes:

  • From loss to score: dLᵢ/dzᵢ = pᵢ − yᵢ. The sigmoid's slope p(1 − p) appears in the algebra and cancels against the cross-entropy's 1/p terms, which is the cancellation that kept the gradient alive for confidently wrong neurons.
  • From score to weights: dzᵢ/dw = xᵢ, the point's own coordinates.

Average over all N points and stack the results, and the whole gradient is one line of linear algebra: grad = Xᵀ(p − y) / N. Each point pushes the weights along its own coordinates, by how wrong its probability is.

#Step 4: verify it twice

A hand-derived gradient is a hypothesis. First check: autograd.

Autograd could, in principle, share a mistake with you, for example if you both differentiated the wrong formula. The second check uses no calculus at all: nudge each weight up and down by a tiny ε and measure how much the loss changes, (L(w + ε) − L(w − ε)) / 2ε. This is called a gradient check, and it's done in float64, because with float32 the rounding error swamps a change of size ε.

A relative error around 1e-10 means the formula is right. Errors near 1e-7 are borderline, and anything around 1e-2 means a bug. torch.eye(2) supplies the two directions to nudge in, one per weight.

#Step 5: gradient descent by hand

Now the training loop, with nothing hidden: forward, gradient, update, repeat. We'll record every weight vector so we can draw the path.

The loss falls quickly from 1.67 and then levels off at 0.3673, the lowest this model can reach on this data. The weights settle near (1.08, 1.07), almost equal, which makes sense: the two centers sit on the diagonal, so both coordinates matter equally. 84.5% accuracy is about what overlapping clouds allow.

#Step 6: see the path

Two panels: on the left, the loss surface over every possible (w₁, w₂) with the paths for two learning rates; on the right, the data with the boundary the trained neuron draws, where z = 0 and p = 0.5.

The surface is computed in one shot: grid holds 22,500 candidate weight pairs as rows, and X @ grid.T scores every point under every pair at once, a (200, 22500) tensor. That's broadcasting and matrix multiplication from Module 2 doing real work. The boundary on the right is the line where w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ = 0, so x₂ = −(w₁/w₂)·x₁.

#Step 7: sweep the learning rate

One run tells you little about the learning rate. A sweep trains the same model from the same start with many learning rates for a fixed budget of steps and plots where each one ends up. Spacing the rates evenly on a log scale covers several orders of magnitude with a dozen runs.

Read it from left to right. Below about 0.3 the loss is still falling when the budget runs out: those rates are safe but slow. From roughly 0.6 to 10, every run reaches the minimum. Past that, the steps overshoot the bowl, just like the opening trace in the Notes, and the loss ends far higher. In practice you pick a rate comfortably inside the flat region, not right at its edge, because a real network's curvature changes during training.

#Step 8: hand the loop to torch.optim

PyTorch packages this loop. nn.Linear(2, 1, bias=False) holds the two weights, autograd computes the gradient, and torch.optim.SGD applies w ← w − lr · grad. We copy in the same starting weights so the two versions can be compared number for number.

Same weights to five decimal places. Those five numbered lines are the core of every training loop in this course, and in Module 4 they get wrapped in batches and epochs. The order matters, and the first line is the one people drop. Watch what the loss does without it:

Instead of settling at 0.367, the loss swings up and down. Each step uses the sum of every gradient so far, which acts like momentum with no friction: the weights keep sliding past the minimum. Nothing crashes, and nothing warns you.

#The finished program

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the gradient check in Step 4 use float64?

  • Autograd works in any floating dtype; Step 4's first check ran it in float32.

  • With ε = 1e-6, float32 keeps about 7 significant digits, so the difference between the two losses would be mostly noise.

  • torch.eye takes any dtype. We asked for float64 to match the data.

Show answer

B. With ε = 1e-6, float32 keeps about 7 significant digits, so the difference between the two losses would be mostly noise.

2In the sweep, a learning rate of 0.04 ended at a loss of about 1.15 after 30 steps. What does that tell you?

  • The loss went down from 1.67, just not far. Divergence would push it up.

  • It's on the crawl side of the curve. The descent is working, only slowly.

  • Other rates reached 0.367 with the same model, so the model isn't the limit.

Show answer

B. It's on the crawl side of the curve. The descent is working, only slowly.

3You forget optimizer.zero_grad(). Why doesn't PyTorch raise an error?

  • .backward() always adds into .grad. Whether that's a bug depends on your intent, which only you know.

  • It doesn't, which is exactly why the loss in Step 8 swung up and down.

  • PyTorch doesn't check whether training is going well; it only runs what you wrote.

Show answer

A. .backward() always adds into .grad. Whether that's a bug depends on your intent, which only you know.

Key takeaways

  • For a sigmoid neuron with cross-entropy, the gradient is Xᵀ(p − y) / N: each point pushes along its own coordinates, by how wrong its probability is.
  • Verify a hand-derived gradient against autograd and against finite differences in float64; a relative error near 1e-10 means it's right.
  • A learning-rate sweep on a log scale shows the crawl, the working range, and the cliff. Pick a rate well inside the working range.
  • The five-line loop is zero_grad, forward, loss, backward, step, and a missing zero_grad fails silently.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a bias weight (append a column of ones to X) and check that the gradient formula still works unchanged.
  • Move the cluster centers apart until the classes don't overlap, then train for 500 steps and watch the weights grow without limit. Why does the loss keep shrinking but never reach 0?
  • Swap torch.optim.SGD for torch.optim.SGD(..., momentum=0.9) and redraw the path on the contour plot.

#Further reading

  • PyTorch: torch.optim (opens in a new tab): how optimizers are constructed, the zero_grad and step contract, and the other algorithms you can swap in.
  • CS231n: Gradient checks (opens in a new tab): Stanford's practical rules for numerical gradient checking, including the relative error thresholds used above.

m3-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Compute mean squared error and cross-entropy by hand, including a version that can't overflow.
  • Explain what applying softmax before F.cross_entropy does to the loss and its gradient.
  • Derive gradients with the chain rule and confirm them with autograd.
  • Write manual weight updates that autograd accepts.
  • Predict the largest stable learning rate for a quadratic loss, and test the prediction.
  • Backpropagate through a two-layer network with matrix formulas.

Every exercise here ends with a check, usually torch.allclose against autograd or a number you predicted. Get in the habit: in deep learning, a wrong gradient doesn't crash anything, it just trains badly, so a check is the only way you'll know.

#Warm-up: two losses on paper

Without code: (a) predictions [2, 4] against targets [3, 1] under mean squared error; (b) cross-entropy when the model gives probabilities [0.7, 0.2, 0.1] and the true class is 1. Then check:

(a) is ((−1)² + 3²) / 2 = 5. (b) looks only at the true class's probability, 0.2, so it's −ln 0.2 ≈ 1.609. The 0.7 given to the wrong class matters only because it took probability away from the right one.

#Exercise 1: cross-entropy that can't overflow

Write my_cross_entropy(logits, targets) for a batch of logits (N, C) and integer targets (N,). First write it the obvious way (exp, divide by the sum, take −log), then test it on [[1000.0, 0.0, -1000.0]] with target 0. Fix it so it matches F.cross_entropy on both ordinary logits and that extreme one.

Need a hint?

exp(1000) is inf in float32. Softmax gives the same answer if you subtract any constant from every logit in a row. Which constant makes the largest exponent exp(0) = 1? Then use −log softmax = log(sum of exps) − (true logit).

Show solution

The naive version computes exp(1000) = inf, then inf / inf = nan. Subtracting each row's maximum keeps every exponent at most exp(0) = 1:

shifted[torch.arange(N), targets] picks one entry per row: row i, column targets[i]. This "subtract the max" trick (the log-sum-exp trick) is what F.cross_entropy does internally, and it's why you should pass it logits instead of computing probabilities yourself.

#Exercise 2: the softmax-before-the-loss bug

A classmate's network ends in nn.Softmax(dim=1), and they pass its output to F.cross_entropy. Their loss never drops below about 0.55, even when every prediction is right. For the confident, correct logits [[10.0, 0.0, 0.0]] (target 0), print the loss with and without the extra softmax, then calculate the lowest loss the buggy version could ever reach with 3 classes.

Need a hint?

After the extra softmax, the "logits" handed to F.cross_entropy are probabilities, so each is between 0 and 1. The best case is [1, 0, 0]. What is the cross-entropy of those logits for class 0?

Show solution

With the extra softmax, the best possible input is [1, 0, 0], and its cross-entropy is −log(e / (e + 2)) = log(1 + 2/e) ≈ 0.5514. The loss has a floor it can never get under, and the gradients reaching the network shrink because they pass through a second softmax. Remove the softmax layer and let F.cross_entropy handle it. When you need probabilities for display, apply softmax to the logits outside the loss.

#Exercise 3: a tanh neuron by hand

For ŷ = tanh(w·x + b) and L = (ŷ − y)², with x = 0.5, y = 0.8, w = 1.5, b = −0.2: derive dL/dw and dL/db, compute them with plain Python math, and confirm with autograd.

Need a hint?

Three links: dL/dŷ = 2(ŷ − y), then the tanh's slope 1 − ŷ² (from Module 2), then x for w or 1 for b.

Show solution

dL/dw = 2(ŷ − y)(1 − ŷ²)·x and dL/db = 2(ŷ − y)(1 − ŷ²).

upstream is the gradient that has flowed back to the weighted sum. Both weights reuse it, which is backpropagation's saving in miniature. The prediction (0.50) is too low, so both gradients are negative: raise w and b to raise ŷ.

#Exercise 4: an update autograd refuses

This hand-written gradient descent step crashes. Read the error, then fix the loop so it runs 50 steps and drives w to the value that makes 2w = 4.

Sample output after the fix:

Need a hint?

Autograd tracks every operation on w so it can differentiate later. The update itself must not be tracked. Which context manager turns tracking off? And something else has to happen to w.grad after each step.

Show solution

w is a leaf: a tensor you created, rather than one computed from others. Changing a tracked leaf in place would corrupt the record autograd needs, so PyTorch refuses unless the change happens inside torch.no_grad(). This is exactly what optimizer.step() does for you, and w.grad.zero_() is what optimizer.zero_grad() does.

#Exercise 5: predict the largest stable learning rate

For the model ŷ = w·x with squared error on x = [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5] and y = 1.2x, the curvature of the loss is 2 · mean(x²). Predict the largest learning rate that converges, then run 50 steps of gradient descent from w = 0 at 0.9× and 1.1× your prediction.

Need a hint?

mean(x²) = (0.25 + 1 + 2.25 + 4 + 6.25) / 5. Convergence needs lr < 2 / curvature.

Show solution

Each step multiplies the distance from w = 1.2 by 1 − lr · 5.5. At 0.9× the limit that factor is −0.8, so the distance shrinks by a fifth each step; at 1.1× it's −1.2, and after 50 steps the error has grown by a factor of about 9,000, so the loss (its square) explodes. A 20% change in learning rate flips training from perfect to useless, which is why the cliff in a learning-rate sweep is so sharp.

#Exercise 6: why classifiers don't use squared error

Train the sigmoid neuron from the Build-along on the same blobs data, starting from the confidently wrong weights w = (−3, −3), for 100 steps at lr = 0.5. Do it once with F.mse_loss(torch.sigmoid(z), y) and once with F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(z, y), record accuracy every step, and plot both.

Need a hint?

Use the Exercise 4 pattern: loss.backward(), then update inside torch.no_grad(), then w.grad.zero_(). Accuracy is the share of points where (z > 0) matches the label.

Show solution

At w = (−3, −3) most points have scores far from zero on the wrong side, where the sigmoid is flat. Squared error's gradient passes through that flat slope and nearly vanishes, so after 100 steps the neuron is still almost entirely wrong. Cross-entropy's gradient is p − y, which is largest exactly when the model is most wrong. Same model, same data, same learning rate; only the loss changed.

#Challenge: backpropagate through two layers by hand

A tiny network: h = X W₁ᵀ + b₁, a = ReLU(h), out = a W₂ᵀ + b₂, with loss L = mean((out − y)²). Use X of shape (8, 3), W₁ (4, 3), b₁ (4,), W₂ (1, 4), b₂ (1,), all from torch.manual_seed(0). Compute the gradients of all four parameter tensors using only matrix operations (no .backward() in your formulas), then compare each with autograd.

Need a hint?

Work backward and keep every gradient the same shape as the thing it's the gradient of. Start with d_out = 2(out − y) / N, shape (8, 1). For a layer out = a Wᵀ + b: dW = d_outᵀ a, db = d_out.sum(0), and the gradient passed back is d_a = d_out W. ReLU passes gradient only where h > 0.

Show solution

The shape rule does most of the work: there's usually only one way to multiply the available tensors that produces the right shape. Biases sum over the batch because every example adds the same bias. And d_h = d_a * (h > 0) is the dead-unit story from Module 2 in one line: where h ≤ 0, no gradient reaches W₁.
