What you'll learn

  • Serve examples with a Dataset and batch them with a DataLoader, including the short last batch.
  • Write train_one_epoch and evaluate functions around the five-line update.
  • Explain what model.train(), model.eval(), and torch.no_grad() each switch, and why you need both kinds.
  • Log an epoch-average training loss and a validation loss, never just the last batch.
  • Diagnose overfitting, a too-small learning rate, and a too-large one from loss curves.

A training script runs for 60 epochs and finishes by printing:

It looks like a triumph. It's nearly meaningless. That number is the loss on the last batch of the last epoch: here, the 8 images left over when 200 training digits are split into batches of 32. It says nothing about the other 192, and nothing at all about digits the model has never seen. By the end of this lesson you'll run that exact training setup and find that its loss on new digits got worse for the final 43 epochs while that printout kept shrinking.

Fixing this takes a loop that measures properly. First, the machinery that feeds it.

#A Dataset answers "give me example i"

PyTorch splits data handling in two. A Dataset knows how many examples there are and how to produce example number i. A DataLoader draws examples from it in shuffled batches. Here's a custom Dataset for the digits; for real image folders, __getitem__ is where you'd open a file from disk.

The two required methods are __len__ and __getitem__. The validation set (25% of the digits, never trained on) is what tells you whether the model works on new data. When you only have tensors already in memory, torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(X, y) does the same job in one line.

#A DataLoader shuffles and batches

1,347 training images in batches of 64 gives 21 full batches and one batch of just 3. The loader stacks individual examples into a batch tensor, (64, 1, 8, 8), so your model never sees one example at a time. Here's what the loader does with indices, in plain Python, over two epochs:

Each epoch visits every example exactly once in a new order, and the leftovers form a short final batch. Shuffling the training set stops the model from learning anything about the order of the data. The validation loader doesn't shuffle, because order can't affect a measurement.

#The five lines, wrapped in epochs

Two functions, reused for the rest of the course:

Three details carry the honesty. loss.item() turns the loss into a plain number, so the running total doesn't hold on to the computation graph. Multiplying by len(yb) weights each batch by its size, so the 3-image batch counts as 3 images and not as a twenty-second of the epoch. And argmax(dim=1) picks a class per row.

#train() and eval(): same weights, different behavior

Some layers act differently while training. Dropout zeroes a random fraction of values during training, which forces the network not to depend on any single unit, and scales the survivors up to keep the average the same. At evaluation time it must do nothing. model.train() and model.eval() flip that behavior for every such layer in the model:

In train mode about half the values become 0 and the rest become 2, so the expected value is still 1. In eval mode the input passes through unchanged. Batch normalization, a layer common in CNNs, also behaves differently in the two modes.

torch.no_grad() is a separate switch: it stops autograd from recording operations, which saves memory and time when you don't need gradients. eval() doesn't turn off gradients, and no_grad() doesn't turn off dropout. Validation needs both, which is why evaluate uses both.

#Run it: the curves behind that printout

Here's the setup from the opening: an oversized network (two hidden layers of 256 units, about 85,000 parameters) trained on only 200 digits. We record every batch's loss, the epoch averages, and the validation numbers.

Both panels cut off the first few epochs, where the loss starts near 2.3. The gray dots are single-batch losses, the kind of number the original script printed. Early on they scatter widely around the blue average, because a batch of 32 is a small, noisy sample. The real story is the gap between blue and orange. The training loss heads to zero: with 85,000 weights and 200 examples, the network can memorize every one. The validation loss bottoms out early and then rises, so the model gets worse on new digits even as it gets "better" on old ones. That's overfitting, and the dashed line marks the epoch you'd want to keep.

Notice that validation accuracy barely moves while validation loss climbs. The model is still right about as often, but it's becoming more and more confident about the digits it gets wrong, and cross-entropy charges heavily for confident mistakes. Loss curves often reveal trouble before accuracy does.

#A field guide to loss curves

What you see Likely cause First thing to try
Train and validation both falling, still falling at the end Not done yet Train longer
Both flat and high from the start Learning rate far too small, or a bug that stops updates Check optimizer.step() runs; raise the learning rate 10×
Loss stuck at about 2.30 with 10 classes The model is guessing uniformly: ln 10 = 2.30 Check labels, inputs, and that gradients reach the weights
Spikes, then nan Learning rate too large Lower it 3 to 10×; check inputs for NaN
Train falls, validation turns upward Overfitting Keep the best epoch; add data, dropout, or weight decay
Validation better than train early on Dropout is active only during training, and train is averaged over a changing epoch Usually fine; compare after a few epochs

#Bugs that hide in training loops

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting to switch back to model.train(). If evaluate calls model.eval() and the training loop never calls model.train(), dropout is off from the second epoch onward. Nothing crashes; the model just trains differently than you think. Putting model.train() as the first line of train_one_epoch makes this impossible.

  • total += loss instead of total += loss.item(). The tensor keeps a reference to its whole computation graph, so memory grows every batch until the GPU runs out.
  • Averaging batch means equally. With a tiny last batch, sum(batch_losses) / len(batch_losses) gives that batch far too much weight. Weight by batch size.
  • Choosing epochs or settings by test accuracy. Validation data is for decisions; the test set is touched once, at the very end.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A training set of 1,000 images uses batch_size=64. How many batches are in one epoch, and how big is the last?

  • A DataLoader keeps the leftovers by default. Only drop_last=True discards them.

  • 15 × 64 = 960, leaving a 16th batch of 40.

  • The loader doesn't rebalance; every batch is full except possibly the last.

Show answer

B. 15 × 64 = 960, leaving a 16th batch of 40.

2Your validation loop uses with torch.no_grad(): but never calls model.eval(). The model has dropout. What's wrong with the validation numbers?

  • no_grad only stops gradient tracking. Dropout still drops units until model.eval() turns it off.

  • The two switches are independent. You need both.

  • Nothing updates the weights without optimizer.step(). The problem is the dropout noise.

Show answer

A. no_grad only stops gradient tracking. Dropout still drops units until model.eval() turns it off.

3Training loss falls steadily for 50 epochs. Validation loss falls until epoch 12, then rises. Which checkpoint should you keep?

  • Training loss measures memorization as well as learning. After epoch 12, the extra drop is memorization.

  • That's the model that does best on data it didn't train on, which is the job.

  • It's the normal signature of overfitting, not a bug.

Show answer

B. That's the model that does best on data it didn't train on, which is the job.

4With 10 classes, the loss of an untrained model is 2.31 and stays at 2.30 for every epoch. What does that suggest?

  • A too-high rate makes the loss jump around or blow up, not sit perfectly still.

  • Overfitting needs training loss to fall. Here nothing is learned at all.

  • ln(10) ≈ 2.30 is the loss of a uniform guess. A flat line there points to a broken loop, not a hard problem.

Show answer

C. ln(10) ≈ 2.30 is the loss of a uniform guess. A flat line there points to a broken loop, not a hard problem.

Key takeaways

  • A Dataset returns example i; a DataLoader shuffles it into batches, and the last batch may be small.
  • Every epoch: model.train() and update on training batches, then model.eval() with torch.no_grad() to measure validation.
  • Log epoch averages weighted by batch size, for both training and validation. A last-batch loss is noise.
  • Training loss falling while validation loss rises is overfitting; keep the epoch with the lowest validation loss.

#Further reading

  • PyTorch: Datasets and DataLoaders (opens in a new tab): writing a custom Dataset for image files on disk, and the DataLoader options worth knowing.
  • PyTorch: Optimizing model parameters (opens in a new tab): the official train and test loops, with the same structure as the functions above.
  • Google: Interpreting loss curves (opens in a new tab): a gallery of curve shapes and what each one usually means.

What you'll learn

  • Split data into training, validation, and test sets, and say what each one is for.
  • Run two sanity checks before training: the starting loss and overfitting a single batch.
  • Train with per-epoch logging and keep the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss.
  • Plot loss and accuracy curves from a real run and read them.
  • Score the test set once, and look at the actual mistakes.

This build puts Modules 2 to 4 together into one complete, honest training run. The finished notebook trains a small network on the 1,797 scikit-learn digits, logs training and validation numbers every epoch, keeps the best weights it has seen, draws its own learning curves, and ends with one test-set score and a picture of every digit it got wrong. Here's the plan:

Start a Colab notebook called m4-l2-digits.ipynb. The whole run takes a few seconds on a CPU, so the GPU is optional here.

#Step 1: split three ways

You need three groups of examples, each with one job. The training set changes the weights. The validation set picks among choices: which epoch, which learning rate. The test set gives one final, unbiased score after every choice is made. Use the test set for decisions and it stops being unbiased, because you've tuned to it.

Splitting index numbers instead of the data itself lets us cut X and y the same way with one list. stratify keeps all ten digits in the same proportions in every group, and random_state makes the split repeat exactly.

#Step 2: wrap the splits in loaders

The data already sits in tensors, so TensorDataset replaces the custom class from the Notes. Only the training loader shuffles.

#Step 3: two checks before you train

The model is a small network with one hidden layer and dropout:

Check 1: the starting loss. An untrained network should be unsure about everything, giving each of 10 classes roughly a 1-in-10 chance, so its cross-entropy should be close to −ln(1/10) = 2.303. It is. A starting loss of 8 or 20 would mean the initial logits are far too large, usually from unscaled inputs, and training would waste its first epochs undoing that.

Check 2: overfit one batch. A healthy model with a working loop can memorize 32 examples almost perfectly. If it can't, the bug is in the model, the loss, or the loop, and no amount of data will fix it.

The loss falls from 2.30 to nearly zero and accuracy on the 32 examples is perfect. Both checks take seconds, and between them they rule out most of the bugs that would otherwise surface as a mysteriously bad curve an hour later.

#Step 4: the loop, with logging and a best checkpoint

These are the functions from the Notes, slightly condensed:

Now train for 40 epochs. After each epoch, if the validation loss is the best so far, save a copy of the weights:

copy.deepcopy matters. model.state_dict() hands back references to the live weight tensors, so without the copy, best_state would keep changing as training continued and you'd end up "restoring" the final weights.

The log shows a fast start (validation accuracy jumps from about 72% to 95% in five epochs), then slow, steady gains.

#Step 5: plot the curves

The log scale on the loss axis makes the late, small improvements visible; on a linear axis everything after epoch 10 would look flat. For the first several epochs, validation loss is actually below training loss. That's the dropout row of the field guide: training is measured with units being dropped, and the training average also includes the worse weights from early in each epoch. Compare with the overfitting run in the Notes: there, validation loss turned upward while training loss kept falling. Here the two curves stay together, the best epoch is the last one, and the field guide's verdict is "not done yet." Dropout and five times as much training data both help. Try 80 epochs yourself and see whether validation loss finally turns.

#Step 6: load the best weights and test once

This is the one number you report. The test loss is a little higher than the best validation loss, and that's expected: the validation set helped choose the checkpoint, so it flatters the model slightly, while the test set played no part in any decision. The checkpoint is saved too; in Colab, point that path into your Drive as in Module 1.

#Step 7: look at the mistakes

An accuracy number hides which errors the model makes. Draw them:

Read the pairs. Several mistakes are digits a person would hesitate over at 8 × 8 pixels, and the confusions are between shapes that share strokes: 1 and 8, 3 and 5, 5 and 6. When you see a pattern in these pictures, you've found where more data or a better architecture would help. A network that ignores where pixels sit relative to each other has to learn every stroke at every position separately, which is the limitation convolutional networks fix in Module 5.

#The finished program

This version folds both loops into one run_epoch. model.train(False) is the same as model.eval(), and torch.set_grad_enabled(False) is the same as torch.no_grad(), so a single flag switches everything.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the best-checkpoint code use copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()) instead of model.state_dict()?

  • You can call it any time. The problem is what it returns.

  • The dictionary would point at the same tensors the optimizer updates. deepcopy freezes a snapshot.

  • It makes a full copy, using as much memory as the weights themselves.

Show answer

B. The dictionary would point at the same tensors the optimizer updates. deepcopy freezes a snapshot.

2A new model's starting loss on 10 classes is 14.2 instead of about 2.3. What's the most likely cause?

  • Shuffled labels change what's learned, but a random model is equally unsure about any labeling, so the starting loss would still be near 2.3.

  • Large logits make the softmax confidently wrong about many examples, and cross-entropy charges heavily for that.

  • The starting loss is measured before any update, so the learning rate hasn't had a chance to matter.

Show answer

B. Large logits make the softmax confidently wrong about many examples, and cross-entropy charges heavily for that.

3Your test accuracy is 0.975 and your best checkpoint's validation accuracy was 0.983. Should you go back and tune until the test score matches?

  • A small gap is expected: the validation set helped pick the checkpoint, so it's slightly optimistic.

  • Report the test number as it is. If you change the model, you need fresh test data to score it fairly.

  • Any choice made by looking at test results leaks information from the test set into the model.

Show answer

B. Report the test number as it is. If you change the model, you need fresh test data to score it fairly.

Key takeaways

  • Three splits, three jobs: training changes weights, validation makes choices, and the test set is scored once at the end.
  • Before training, check that the starting loss is about ln(number of classes) and that the model can overfit one batch.
  • Log per-epoch training and validation loss and accuracy, and keep a deepcopy of the weights with the lowest validation loss.
  • After the test score, look at the actual mistakes; they tell you what to try next.

  • Train for 80 epochs and find out whether validation loss ever turns upward with dropout at 0.2. Then set dropout to 0 and compare.
  • Add early stopping: end training when validation loss hasn't improved for 8 epochs.
  • In Colab, scale the same loop up to the full 28 × 28 MNIST dataset (60,000 training images) on the T4. Only the data loading and the first layer change:

What you'll learn

  • Predict a classifier's starting loss and use it to catch bad initialization.
  • Compute epoch averages and accuracy correctly, and spot the versions that are subtly wrong.
  • Find bugs in a training loop that raise no errors.
  • Predict the shape of loss curves for different learning rates and data sizes, then check.
  • Build early stopping and a learning-rate range test, and use both on a real overfitting problem.

These exercises build on each other, so this lesson works like one notebook: run the setup cell first, and later exercises reuse the functions from earlier ones. Most of the bugs here produce no error message at all. That's the point: the training loop is where silent bugs live.

#Warm-up: what should the first loss be?

An untrained classifier spreads its probability roughly evenly, so its cross-entropy starts near −ln(1/C) = ln C for C classes. Predict the starting loss for 2, 10, and 26 classes, then check:

If your 10-class model starts at 2.3, initialization is sane. If it starts at 15, the logits are huge, usually because inputs weren't scaled, and the first epochs will be spent undoing that.

#Setup: data and a training helper

Run this once. It splits the digits into training and validation sets and defines train_run, which trains a two-hidden-layer network with the settings you give it and returns per-epoch history.

#Exercise 1: the honest epoch average

A loader produced three batches with these mean losses and sizes. Compute the naive average of the three numbers and the correct per-example average.

Need a hint?

The correct average gives every example equal weight. Each batch mean stands for size examples, so multiply before you add, then divide by the total number of examples.

Show solution

The 3-example batch, probably a few odd digits left over at the end of an epoch, nearly triples the naive figure. Weighting it by its size gives those 3 examples the influence of 3 examples. If you set drop_last=True on the training loader, every batch is the same size and the two averages agree.

#Exercise 2: accuracy that's only wrong sometimes

This accuracy function runs without complaint on a batch of 10, where every prediction is right, and reports 0.0. On a batch of 16 it crashes. Explain both results, then fix it.

Need a hint?

logits has shape (batch, classes). Which dimension does argmax(dim=0) collapse, and what shape is left? Why does that shape happen to match the labels when the batch size is 10?

Show solution

argmax(dim=0) finds the highest-scoring example for each class, giving one number per class, shape (10,). With a batch of 10 that matches the labels' shape by coincidence, so the comparison runs and returns a wrong answer. With 16 examples it's (10,) against (16,), which can't broadcast. The class dimension is 1:

The crash was the lucky case. Batch size equal to the number of classes is rare, but when it happens this bug reports a believable, wrong accuracy with no error at all. Test metric code on a batch size that differs from every other dimension.

#Exercise 3: two silent bugs

This loop trains, prints, and never errors. It also has two bugs. The prints give both away; find them and fix the loop.

Need a hint?

Bug 1: what does validate leave the model in, and who switches it back? Bug 2: what kind of object does running become after the first += loss, and what does it keep a reference to?

Show solution

Bug 1: validate calls model.eval(), and nothing calls model.train() again, so dropout is off for epochs 1 and 2. Bug 2: running += loss turns running into a tensor that's part of the autograd graph, so every batch's graph stays in memory until the epoch ends. On a GPU with a large model, that's how you run out of memory halfway through an epoch. The fix moves model.train() inside the epoch loop and uses .item():

Putting model.train() at the top of each epoch means no helper function can leave the model in the wrong mode.

#Exercise 4: predict the curves, then train

Using train_run, four runs are planned. Before running anything, sketch the training and validation loss curves you expect for each over 40 epochs:

  • A: lr=0.001
  • B: lr=0.1
  • C: lr=2.0
  • D: lr=0.05, momentum=0.9, but only n_train=150 examples and a much wider network, width=512

Then run all four and plot them side by side.

Need a hint?

Think back to the learning-rate sweep in Module 3: where on that curve do 0.001 and 2.0 sit? For D, compare the number of weights with the number of training examples.

Show solution

A is the crawl: correct direction, far too small steps, still near ln 10 after 40 epochs. B is healthy: both curves fall together. The occasional validation spikes come from the last few batches of an epoch knocking the weights off course, with the next epoch recovering. Spikes on an otherwise good curve hint that the learning rate is near the top of its safe range, and Exercise 6 will agree. C is the interesting one. It doesn't produce nan; a few huge early steps push most ReLU units into the dead zone, and the network is left predicting roughly uniform probabilities, stuck at 2.3 forever. That's the "stuck at about 2.30" row of the field guide, caused by a learning rate rather than a bug in the code. D is overfitting: the training loss heads for zero, and the validation loss turns upward after its best epoch.

#Exercise 5: early stopping

Write a class EarlyStopper(patience) with a method step(val_loss) that returns True when training should stop: when the validation loss hasn't set a new best for patience epochs in a row. It should also remember the best epoch. Test it on this sequence with patience=3:

Need a hint?

Keep three numbers: the best loss so far, the epoch it happened, and a counter of epochs since then. A new best resets the counter to 0; anything else adds 1.

Show solution

Epoch 4 (0.62) is worse than 0.60, but epoch 5 sets a new best and resets the counter, so a single bad epoch doesn't end training. Epochs 6, 7, and 8 all fail to beat 0.58, and it stops. In a real loop you'd save a deepcopy of the weights whenever best_epoch changes, and load them after stopping. Patience trades time for safety: validation loss is noisy, so a patience of 1 stops on the first unlucky epoch.

#Exercise 6: a learning-rate range test

Instead of guessing a learning rate, measure. Train for 100 batches while multiplying the learning rate by a constant factor every batch, from 1e-4 up to 10. Record a smoothed loss at each step and stop early if it climbs above 4 times the best so far. Plot loss against learning rate on a log axis.

Need a hint?

The factor is (10 / 1e-4) ** (1 / 100). Set the rate each step with for group in optimizer.param_groups: group["lr"] = lr. For smoothing, keep smooth = 0.8 * smooth + 0.2 * loss.item().

Show solution

Below about 0.3 the steps are too small to move the loss in 100 batches. The loss reaches its lowest point near 1.8, then turns bumpy and explodes (the chart clips the final spike). The rule of thumb is to pick a rate about ten times smaller than the minimum, giving 0.18 here: just above run B in Exercise 4, which trained well with a few spikes, and about 11 times below run C, which broke. A range test costs about one-sixth of an epoch's worth of compute, far less than a sweep of full runs.

#Challenge: beat the overfitter without more data

Run D from Exercise 4 overfit badly. Keep its data (150 examples), width (512), and optimizer settings, and improve its best validation loss using any mix of dropout, weight_decay (which shrinks every weight a little at each step), and early stopping with your EarlyStopper. Report the baseline and your version side by side: best validation loss, the accuracy at that epoch, and the epoch where early stopping would have ended training.

Need a hint?

Dropout makes memorizing individual examples harder; weight decay keeps weights small. Try dropout=0.5 with weight_decay=1e-3 for 60 epochs, then replay each run's validation losses through an EarlyStopper(patience=8).

Show solution

The regularized network reaches a lower best validation loss and a higher accuracy at that point. Early stopping helps both runs differently: for the baseline it ends training soon after the turn, while the regularized network keeps improving for longer because it's slower to memorize. The improvement is real but modest, which is the honest lesson: with 150 examples, regularization can only do so much. More data, or a model that bakes in what images look like (Module 5's convolutions), moves the needle further.

What you'll learn

  • Compute one output of a convolution by hand and check it against F.conv2d.
  • Predict a layer's output size with ⌊(n + 2p − k) / s⌋ + 1.
  • Count a convolution layer's parameters and explain weight sharing.
  • Say what max pooling keeps, what it throws away, and why that helps with small shifts.
  • Choose augmentations from torchvision.transforms.v2 that keep the label true.

Here is a fully connected network, the kind you trained in Module 4, on the 8×8 handwritten digits. It does well on the test set. Then we slide every test image one pixel to the right and score it again. Nothing else changes.

To you, a 3 moved one pixel over is still a 3. To this network it's a different input. Its first layer has a separate weight for every pixel position, so "ink at row 2, column 5" and "ink at row 2, column 6" are unrelated facts. It learned where the ink usually sits, not what the strokes look like.

A convolutional network builds in a different assumption: a stroke means the same thing wherever it appears. The rest of this page is the machinery that makes that assumption work.

#A kernel is a small pattern you slide across the image

Here's the intuition. Hold a 3×3 stencil of numbers over the top-left corner of the image. Multiply each stencil number by the pixel under it and add the nine products. The sum says how well that patch matches the stencil. Slide one pixel right and repeat, row by row. The grid of sums is called a feature map, and the stencil is the kernel (or filter).

Now precisely. For an image I, a k×k kernel K, and a bias b:

Take a 5×5 image that is dark (0) on the left and bright (9) in its last two columns, and the kernel below, which subtracts the left column of the patch from the right column. At the window starting in column 1, each row of the patch is 0, 0, 9, so each row contributes −1·0 + 0·0 + 1·9 = 9, and three rows give 27. Check it with PyTorch:

The output is 3×3, not 5×5, because a 3-wide window fits in only three positions across five columns. Where the window sits on flat dark pixels the answer is 0; where it straddles the edge, it's 27.

📝 Note

Mathematicians flip the kernel before sliding it; that's "true" convolution. PyTorch and every other deep-learning library skip the flip (strictly, it's cross-correlation). Since the network learns its kernels, the flip makes no difference, and everyone calls it convolution anyway.

Step through the same sliding window written as plain loops. Watch total build up for each position, then land in row:

#An edge detector on a picture

The same arithmetic finds edges in a real picture. Below, two kernels go into one conv2d call as two output channels, so we get two feature maps at once. The first is the Sobel kernel for left-to-right changes (vertical edges), and the second is the same kernel turned on its side.

Inside each shape and in the background the patch is flat, so the kernel's positive and negative halves cancel to 0. On a left edge the patch goes dark-to-bright and the response is positive (red). A right edge gives the same size response with the opposite sign (blue). A CNN's first layer learns kernels much like these on its own, because edges are the cheapest clue to what's in an image.

#Stride and padding set the output size

Two settings change how the window moves:

  • Padding p adds p rows and columns of zeros around the border, so the window can be centered on edge pixels.
  • Stride s is how many pixels the window jumps each move. Stride 2 skips every other position and roughly halves the height and width.

For an input of size n and a kernel of size k, the output size is

For an 8×8 digit with a 3×3 kernel: no padding gives (8 − 3)/1 + 1 = 6. Padding 1 gives (8 + 2 − 3)/1 + 1 = 8, the same size as the input. Padding 1 with stride 2 gives ⌊7/2⌋ + 1 = 4. Check the formula against real layers:

The rule of thumb: kernel 3 with padding 1 (or kernel 5 with padding 2) keeps the size, which PyTorch also lets you write as padding="same" when the stride is 1.

#One small detector, shared across every position

A layer like nn.Conv2d(1, 16, kernel_size=3) holds 16 kernels of shape 1×3×3 plus 16 biases: 16 × 9 + 16 = 160 numbers. With C_in input channels, each kernel spans all of them, so the count is C_out × C_in × k × k + C_out. A fully connected layer producing the same 16×8×8 output from an 8×8 input would need 64 × 1,024 + 1,024 = 66,560.

The saving comes from weight sharing: the same 3×3 kernel is used at every position. That has a useful side effect. Shift the input, and the feature map shifts by exactly the same amount. Run a random conv layer both ways:

The two orders agree (only the border columns, where zero padding meets the image, can differ). This property is called translation equivariance. It's why a stroke detector trained on digits near the center still fires on digits near the edge. Notice the word "equivariant", not "invariant": the feature map moves with the input. A layer that later reads that map position by position can still be fooled, which is where pooling and augmentation come in.

#Pooling keeps the strongest nearby response

nn.MaxPool2d(2) splits each feature map into 2×2 blocks and keeps the largest value in each. It has no weights, and it halves height and width.

Both give the same 2×2 result: the pooled map recorded that there's a strong response in the top-left block and threw away exactly where in the block it was. That tolerance only covers moves inside a block. A move across a block boundary still changes the output, so pooling buys a little shift tolerance, not immunity.

#Augmentation: train on the changes you expect

If test images may be shifted, tilted, or dimmer, show the model shifted, tilted, and dimmer training images with the same labels. That's data augmentation: a random, label-preserving change applied every time a training image is loaded, so each epoch sees a slightly different version of each image. You never augment validation or test images; they should look like the real inputs.

torchvision.transforms.v2 provides the transforms. RandomAffine shifts and rotates, ColorJitter changes brightness and contrast:

The test for any augmentation is simple: would a person still give the new image the same label? A small shift of a digit, yes. A horizontal flip of a cat photo, yes. A horizontal flip of a 2 or a 7, no: it becomes a mirror-image shape that isn't a digit, and you'd be training the model on false examples.

⚠️ Watch out

Conv layers expect four dimensions: (batch, channels, height, width). The digits come as (N, 8, 8); forget the channel dimension and PyTorch reads your 64-image batch as one image with 64 channels:

Fix it with images.unsqueeze(1), which inserts the channel axis to make (N, 1, 8, 8).

⚠️ Watch out

A v2 transform called on a whole batch tensor applies the same random change to every image in it. All 64 digits shift by the same amount, which is far less variety than you wanted. Apply the transform to one image at a time, usually inside a Dataset's __getitem__, as the next lesson does.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A batch of 32×32 color images goes through nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=5) (stride 1, no padding). What is the shape of one output?

  • (32 + 0 − 5)/1 + 1 = 28, and the number of channels becomes out_channels, 16.

  • The size would stay 32 only with padding 2 on each side.

  • The output has one channel per kernel, so 16, not the 3 input channels.

Show answer

A. (32 + 0 − 5)/1 + 1 = 28, and the number of channels becomes out_channels, 16.

2How many trainable numbers does nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=5) have?

  • That's 16 × 5 × 5, which forgets that each kernel spans all 3 input channels, and forgets the biases.

  • Right weights (16 × 3 × 5 × 5), but each of the 16 kernels also has a bias.

  • 16 × 3 × 5 × 5 = 1,200 weights plus 16 biases.

Show answer

C. 16 × 3 × 5 × 5 = 1,200 weights plus 16 biases.

3An 8×8 feature map goes through nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1). What height and width come out?

  • Padding 1 keeps the size only at stride 1.

  • ⌊(8 + 2 − 3)/2⌋ + 1 = ⌊3.5⌋ + 1 = 4.

  • That's what you'd get with no padding: ⌊5/2⌋ + 1 = 3.

Show answer

B. ⌊(8 + 2 − 3)/2⌋ + 1 = ⌊3.5⌋ + 1 = 4.

4You're training a classifier for photos of handwritten digits. Which augmentation teaches it something false?

  • A shifted 4 is still a 4, so this is safe and useful.

  • A faded 4 is still a 4.

  • A mirrored 2, 3, or 7 is not a digit at all, yet you'd label it as one.

Show answer

C. A mirrored 2, 3, or 7 is not a digit at all, yet you'd label it as one.

Key takeaways

  • A convolution slides a small kernel across the image and records the sum of products at each position; the result is a feature map.
  • Output size is ⌊(n + 2p − k)/s⌋ + 1. Kernel 3 with padding 1 keeps the size; stride 2 halves it.
  • A conv layer has C_out × C_in × k × k + C_out parameters, far fewer than a dense layer, because one kernel is shared across every position.
  • Shared weights make feature maps shift with the input; max pooling forgives small moves inside each block.
  • Augment only the training data, and only with changes that keep the label true.

#Further reading

  • CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks (opens in a new tab): Stanford's notes, with the clearest explanation of stride, padding, and depth.
  • A guide to convolution arithmetic for deep learning (opens in a new tab): every output-size case drawn as pictures, including transposed convolutions you'll meet in segmentation models.
  • torchvision: Transforming images (opens in a new tab): the official list of v2 transforms and how they handle images, boxes, and masks.

What you'll learn

  • Wrap image tensors in a Dataset that augments one image at a time.
  • Define a two-block CNN and print the shape after every layer.
  • Train an MLP and a CNN with one shared training function and compare their curves.
  • Measure accuracy on shifted test images, then close the gap with transforms.v2.
  • Plot the CNN's learned kernels and the feature maps it makes for one digit.

The last lesson ended on a weak spot: the fully connected network fell apart when the test digits moved one pixel. Here you build the fix and measure how much it helps. This is the network:

By the end you'll have a table comparing three models (an MLP, this CNN, and this CNN trained with augmentation) on the original test digits and on copies shifted one and two pixels. Run the cells in order; each one uses names from the cells before it.

#Step 1: Split the data and make shifted test sets

Three splits this time. Training data fits the weights, validation data is for choices like the number of epochs, and the test set is looked at once, at the end.

Always look at a transformed image before trusting it. A sign error in shift would quietly move the digits the wrong way:

#Step 2: A Dataset that augments one image at a time

A Dataset needs two methods: __len__ and __getitem__. Putting the transform inside __getitem__ means every image gets its own random change each time the DataLoader asks for it, which avoids the whole-batch trap from the last lesson.

#Step 3: Define both models and check the shapes

Two builder functions, so we can make fresh copies with a fixed seed later:

Walking a fake batch through the layers one at a time is the fastest way to get nn.Linear(32 * 2 * 2, 10) right. Padding 1 keeps each conv's output the same size, and each pool halves it: 8 → 4 → 2. The CNN also has fewer parameters than the MLP, thanks to weight sharing.

#Step 4: One training function for every model

fit seeds the random generator before building the model, so the same seed gives the same starting weights and the same batch order. It records the average training loss and the validation accuracy after every epoch.

On the original digits the two models are close. If you stopped here, you'd conclude the CNN isn't worth the extra code.

#Step 5: Score both models on the moved digits

Now the CNN pulls ahead, but it still loses a lot on shifted digits. Shared kernels make the feature maps move with the digit, yet the final Linear layer reads the flattened 2×2 map position by position, and a one-pixel move on an 8-pixel image often crosses a pooling block boundary. The architecture gives tolerance to shifts; it doesn't give immunity.

#Step 6: Add augmentation and train again

If shifted digits are what the model will face, train it on shifted digits. translate=(0.25, 0.25) moves each training image by up to a quarter of its width (2 pixels) in each direction, chosen fresh every time it's loaded. First, look at what the model will actually see:

Every digit is still readable, and a few are pushed right up against the edge. Now train the same CNN architecture on these, with more epochs because the task got harder:

The augmented CNN holds up on every shifted set. It gives up a few points on the original images: it spent some of its capacity learning to handle positions the original test set never uses. That trade-off is normal, and validation accuracy is how you'd tune it (more epochs, a gentler translate, or a wider network).

#Step 7: Look at what the CNN learned

The first conv layer's weights have shape (16, 1, 3, 3): sixteen 3×3 kernels. Plot them, and the sixteen feature maps they produce for one test digit:

Several kernels have a positive side and a negative side, the same shape as the edge filters you built by hand. Each feature map lights up a different part of the digit: some respond to the left edges of strokes, some to the top, some to the inside of loops. Nobody wrote these; gradient descent found them because they help separate the ten classes.

#The finished program

Everything above as one script you can paste into a Colab cell. It picks the GPU when there is one.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the augmentation live inside Digits.__getitem__ instead of being called on xb in the training loop?

  • Speed isn't the reason; calling the transform on a batch would be fewer calls, not more.

  • Calling it per image gives each digit its own random shift, so the model sees far more variety.

  • DataLoader doesn't check where tensors came from.

Show answer

B. Calling it per image gives each digit its own random shift, so the model sees far more variety.

2You want to choose between translate=(0.15, 0.15) and translate=(0.25, 0.25). Which numbers should decide?

  • Choices are made on validation data, so the test set stays an unbiased final check.

  • Picking settings by test score turns the test set into a second validation set, and the final number becomes optimistic.

  • Stronger augmentation makes training harder, so training loss will favor the weaker setting regardless of how well it generalizes.

Show answer

A. Choices are made on validation data, so the test set stays an unbiased final check.

3Without augmentation, which part of the CNN makes it sensitive to where the digit sits?

  • A conv layer's output shifts along with its input, so it doesn't care where a stroke is.

  • ReLU works on each value separately and doesn't involve position at all.

  • It has a separate weight for each position in that map, so the same feature in a different block gives a different score.

Show answer

C. It has a separate weight for each position in that map, so the same feature in a different block gives a different score.

Key takeaways

  • Put random transforms in Dataset.__getitem__ so each image gets its own random change every epoch.
  • Push a fake batch through the layers and print shapes before you train; it's how you size the final Linear.
  • Seed before building the model so runs you compare start from the same weights and see the same batch order.
  • A CNN tolerates small shifts better than an MLP, and augmentation that matches the expected shift closes most of the remaining gap.
  • Augmentation can cost a little accuracy on the unchanged data; tune its strength on validation, not test.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add v2.ColorJitter(contrast=0.5) to the augmentation and test on a low-contrast copy of the test set (X_test * 0.6 + 0.3).
  • Replace nn.Flatten() and the final Linear with nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), and nn.Linear(32, 10), which averages each map over all positions. Does it help with shifts by itself?
  • Train on real photos with your Colab GPU. CIFAR-10 has 60,000 color images, 32×32, in 10 classes. Use nn.Conv2d(3, 16, ...) for the three color channels, and nn.Linear(32 * 8 * 8, 10) because two pools take 32 down to 8. The first run downloads about 170 MB; if Colab shows a download error, run the cell again.

Unlike digits, a horizontal flip is safe here, which is why it appears in train_tf.

  • PyTorch: Training a Classifier (opens in a new tab): the official CIFAR-10 walkthrough; compare its network with yours.
  • Getting started with transforms v2 (opens in a new tab): how v2 handles images, boxes, and masks together, which matters once you augment detection data.
  • Feature Visualization (Distill) (opens in a new tab): what the deeper layers of a large CNN respond to, shown with generated images.

What you'll learn

  • Predict output shapes and parameter counts for conv, pool, and linear layers before running anything.
  • Design kernels that respond to a chosen pattern.
  • Read a shape-mismatch error and fix the layer that caused it.
  • Stress-test a trained CNN with realistic changes, and fix one weakness with a custom augmentation.

Work in one Colab notebook (or run the cells here in order). Try each exercise before opening the solution; the hints are there for when you're stuck for more than a few minutes.

#Warm-up: shapes in your head

A 1×28×28 image goes through Conv2d(1, 8, 5), MaxPool2d(2), Conv2d(8, 16, 3, padding=1), and MaxPool2d(2). Write down the shape after each layer.

Show solution

(8, 24, 24) because 28 − 5 + 1 = 24. Then (8, 12, 12) after pooling. The padded 3×3 conv keeps the size and changes the channels: (16, 12, 12). The last pool gives (16, 6, 6), so a following Linear would need 16 * 6 * 6 = 576 inputs.

The exercises below share this setup cell. It loads the digits and trains the baseline CNN from the build-along, which Exercises 5 and 6 test.

#Exercise 1: Output sizes, including dilation

A dilated convolution spreads its kernel out, leaving gaps of d − 1 pixels between taps, so a 3×3 kernel with dilation=2 covers a 5×5 area. The full output-size rule is:

Write conv_out(n, k, s=1, p=0, d=1) and a unittest test that compares it with the real height of nn.Conv2d outputs for at least 50 random combinations of input size, kernel, stride, padding, and dilation. Skip combinations where the kernel doesn't fit.

Need a hint?

With d = 1 the formula reduces to the one from the notes. Use random.randint for each setting, and self.subTest(...) so a failure tells you which combination broke. A combination is invalid when n + 2p < d*(k - 1) + 1.

Show solution

The - d*(k - 1) - 1 part is the effective kernel size d*(k - 1) + 1 written out; with d = 1 it's just k.

#Exercise 2: Where do the parameters live?

This CNN is for 3×32×32 color images (CIFAR-10 size):

By hand, count the parameters in each layer that has any, and the total. Which layer holds the most? Then count again after replacing Flatten + Linear with nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64, 10). Check both totals in code.

Need a hint?

Use C_out × C_in × k × k + C_out for each conv and in × out + out for each linear. Pooling, ReLU, and Flatten have none.

Show solution

Conv 1: 32 × 3 × 9 + 32 = 896. Conv 2: 64 × 32 × 9 + 64 = 18,496. Linear: 4,096 × 10 + 10 = 40,970. Total 60,362, and the final linear layer holds about two thirds of it. With global average pooling the linear layer shrinks to 64 × 10 + 10 = 650, for a total of 20,042.

This is why most modern CNNs, ResNet included, end with global average pooling: the conv layers are cheap, and a big flattened map feeding a dense layer is where parameters pile up.

#Exercise 3: Design a line detector

Build a 24×24 test image with a bright horizontal line, a bright vertical line, and a bright diagonal on a dark background. Design a 3×3 kernel that responds strongly to horizontal lines (a bright row with dark rows above and below), and weakly to the other two lines. Also make a 3×3 box blur. Apply both with F.conv2d and plot the input and the two outputs. Print the strongest response along each line.

Need a hint?

A kernel gives zero on flat areas when its numbers sum to zero. Put positive weights where the line should be (the middle row) and negative weights above and below. A box blur is all ninths.

Show solution

On the horizontal line the middle row contributes 2 + 2 + 2 and the dark rows contribute nothing: 6. On the vertical line each row of the window holds one bright pixel, so the sum is −1 + 2 − 1 = 0. Centered on the diagonal, the window also holds one bright pixel per row and sums to 0; one pixel to the side it catches the middle-row pixel and only one outer pixel, which leaves 1. A tilted line is a weak, partial match.

#Exercise 4: Fix the crash

This network is meant for the digits, but it crashes on the first batch:

Explain both numbers in (4x32 and 128x10), then fix it two ways: once by correcting in_features, and once without computing it at all.

Need a hint?

Trace the height: no padding means each 3×3 conv shrinks the size by 2. For the second fix, look up nn.LazyLinear in the PyTorch docs.

Show solution

4x32 is the input to the linear layer: 4 images, each flattened to 32 numbers, because 8 → 6 (conv) → 3 (pool) → 1 (conv) leaves a 32×1×1 map. 128x10 is the layer's weight as PyTorch multiplies it: it expects 128 inputs. Fix 1 is nn.Linear(32, 10). Fix 2 is nn.LazyLinear(10), which reads its input size from the first batch:

Run one dummy batch through a lazy model before creating the optimizer; until then its weights don't exist yet.

#Exercise 5: Stress-test the baseline

Real inputs vary in ways your test split doesn't. Build six altered copies of X_test: shifted right one pixel, rotated 15°, faded (X_test * 0.5 + 0.25, a washed-out scan), Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.15 (clamped to 0 to 1), slightly blurred, and flipped left to right. Print the baseline's accuracy on each. Which drop would you fix with augmentation, and which would you leave alone?

Need a hint?

torchvision.transforms.v2.functional has rotate, gaussian_blur, and horizontal_flip, and each one works on a whole batch tensor (here, applying the same change to every image is exactly what you want). Seed before adding noise so your numbers are repeatable.

Show solution

Read the table as a list of risks. The one-pixel shift is the disaster: about half the digits come out wrong. Rotation, fading, and blur each cost several points, and all three are realistic for scanned forms (a crooked page, a faint photocopy, a cheap scanner), so they're worth augmenting. Noise at this level barely matters. The flipped score should stay low: a mirrored digit isn't a valid input, so a model that "handles" flips has learned to read nonsense. (It isn't near 10% because 0, 1, and 8 look much the same mirrored.)

#Exercise 6: Write your own augmentation for faded scans

v2 doesn't have a transform for "washed out toward gray". It doesn't need one: any callable that takes an image and returns an image can go in v2.Compose. Write a class RandomFade(max_lift) that picks a random lift between 0 and max_lift and returns image * (1 - lift) + lift / 2. Train a CNN with v2.Compose([RandomFade(0.6), v2.RandomAffine(degrees=0, translate=(0.15, 0.15))]) and compare it with the baseline on the original, shifted, and faded sets.

Need a hint?

Draw the random number with torch.rand(1).item() rather than Python's random module, so torch.manual_seed controls it. Give the augmented model 30 epochs.

Show solution

Both weak spots improve sharply, at the cost of a few points on the original images. The faded test set (0.5x + 0.25) is exactly what RandomFade produces with lift = 0.5, inside the range the model trained on. In a real project you'd set max_lift from the faintest scans you've actually seen, not from the test set; otherwise you're tuning to the answer.

#Challenge: the smallest robust CNN

Build a CNN for the digits with under 3,000 parameters that scores at least 90% on the original test set and at least 85% on the copy shifted right by two pixels. Report the parameter count, both accuracies, and one sentence on which design choice mattered most.

Need a hint?

Channels are the expensive part: a conv from 16 to 32 channels costs 4,640 parameters on its own, so try 8 and 16. Global average pooling removes most of the final layer's weights. You'll still need translation augmentation, and probably more epochs than 20.

What you'll learn

  • Explain what a pretrained backbone already knows and why a new head needs few labels.
  • Freeze a ResNet-18, replace its final layer, and count what's left to train.
  • Choose between training only the head, fine-tuning the last blocks, and fine-tuning everything.
  • Describe what classification, detection, and segmentation models return.
  • Compute intersection over union (IoU) for boxes, and explain non-maximum suppression.

A school garden club wants an app that tells three tomato-leaf diseases apart, and they've photographed 40 leaves of each. ResNet-18, one of the smaller standard vision networks, has 11.7 million parameters. Train it from scratch on 120 photos and it will memorize every leaf, including the shadows and the table it was photographed on, and learn almost nothing that carries over to a new leaf.

But somebody has already trained ResNet-18 on ImageNet: 1.28 million photos in 1,000 categories. Most of what that network learned isn't about those 1,000 categories at all. It's about edges, textures, and shapes, and leaves have all three. Transfer learning keeps that knowledge and retrains only the part that's specific to the new task.

#What a pretrained network already knows

You saw the first step of this in the last module: the first conv layer of your digit CNN learned edge detectors. A deep network trained on millions of photos stacks many such layers, and each one builds on the one before:

  • Early layers respond to edges, color contrasts, and simple blobs. They're useful for almost any photo.
  • Middle layers combine those into textures and parts: fur, mesh, wheels, veins on a leaf.
  • The last layer maps the final 512 features to ImageNet's 1,000 class scores. That's the only part that is truly about ImageNet.

So the recipe is: keep everything up to the last layer (the backbone), throw away the last layer (the head), and attach a new head with one output per class in your task.

#Look inside ResNet-18

torchvision.models builds the architecture. With weights=None you get random weights and nothing is downloaded, which is enough to look at its structure:

The ten top-level parts are a stem (conv1, bn1, relu, maxpool), four stages of residual blocks (layer1 to layer4), global average pooling (avgpool), and the head (fc): a Linear from 512 features to 1,000 classes.

In Colab you load the real ImageNet weights by passing a weights enum. The weights object also carries the exact preprocessing the network was trained with, so you don't have to remember the resize size or the normalization numbers. The first call downloads about 45 MB; if it stops with a network error, check the runtime is connected and run the cell again.

#Freeze the backbone, replace the head

Freezing means telling autograd not to compute gradients for a parameter, by setting requires_grad = False. Then the head is replaced with a fresh Linear whose output size is your number of classes. New layers are created with requires_grad=True, so only the head will learn:

From 11 million trainable numbers down to 1,539 (512 × 3 weights plus 3 biases). A linear classifier with 1,539 parameters is something 120 photos can train without memorizing. This setting is often called feature extraction: the frozen backbone turns each photo into 512 good features, and you fit a small classifier on top.

#When to fine-tune more than the head

Sometimes the frozen features aren't quite right for your images. Fine-tuning unfreezes some or all of the backbone and keeps training it, gently. The question is how much to unfreeze, and it depends on two things: how much labeled data you have, and how much your images look like ImageNet's everyday photos.

Your data Similar to everyday photos Very different (X-rays, satellite, microscope)
Small (tens to a few hundred per class) Freeze the backbone, train the head Fine-tune the last stage too, with a small learning rate
Large (thousands per class) Fine-tune everything with a small learning rate Fine-tune everything; training from scratch becomes an option

When you do unfreeze, give the pretrained layers a smaller learning rate than the new head. Their weights are already good, and big steps would wreck them before the head has learned anything useful. PyTorch optimizers take a list of parameter groups, each with its own settings:

A common schedule is to train the head alone for a few epochs first, then unfreeze layer4 and continue. Starting fine-tuning with a random head sends large, random gradients into the pretrained layers.

#Beyond one label per image

Classification answers "what is in this photo?" with one label. Many products need more than that: a self-checkout camera needs to know where each item is, and a medical tool may need the exact outline of a lesion. Three tasks, three kinds of output:

Task Answers Output for one image
Classification What is it? One score per class
Object detection What, and where? A list of boxes (x1, y1, x2, y2), each with a label and a confidence score
Semantic segmentation Which class is each pixel? A class score map per class, the same size as the image
Instance segmentation Which pixels belong to each separate object? One mask per object, plus a box, label, and score

Detectors and segmenters are built the same way as your leaf classifier: a pretrained backbone with a task-specific head on top. torchvision ships pretrained versions trained on the COCO dataset. Both downloads are over 150 MB, so if Colab stops with a timeout error, run the cell again:

found["boxes"] has shape (N, 4), one row per detected object, in pixel coordinates. The segmenter returns 21 score maps (20 object classes plus background), and taking argmax over that dimension gives one class per pixel.

#Scoring a box: intersection over union

A predicted box is never exactly the true box, so detection needs a measure of "close enough". Intersection over union divides the area where the two boxes overlap by the area they cover together. Identical boxes score 1; boxes that don't touch score 0. A common convention counts a detection as correct when IoU ≥ 0.5 with a true box of the same class.

Detectors also produce many overlapping boxes for the same object. Non-maximum suppression (NMS) cleans that up: keep the highest-scoring box, delete every other box that overlaps it by more than a threshold, and repeat with what's left. Both are one call in torchvision.ops:

NMS kept box 0 (score 0.92) and box 3 (0.88). Boxes 1 and 2 overlapped box 0 by more than 0.5, so they were dropped even though each of them, alone, would have been a fine detection. The same IoU idea scores segmentation: count the pixels in both masks, divide by the pixels in either.

⚠️ Watch out

A frozen backbone isn't completely frozen in training mode. ResNet's BatchNorm layers update their running mean and variance on every forward pass in model.train(), whether or not requires_grad is set. With a small dataset, those statistics drift away from what the pretrained weights expect, and accuracy at test time drops for no obvious reason. When you train only the head, keep the backbone in eval mode (model.eval(), since the new head has no dropout or BatchNorm of its own).

⚠️ Watch out

Preprocessing must match the pretrained weights. The ImageNet weights expect 224×224 crops normalized with ImageNet's mean and standard deviation. Feed raw 0–255 pixels, or skip the normalization, and the "pretrained" features are nonsense. Use weights.transforms(), or copy its settings into your own v2.Compose.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You have 300 photos of five dog breeds and an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18. What's the best first experiment?

  • Dog photos look like ImageNet (which has many dog breeds), and 300 photos is small, so the frozen features are a strong, cheap start.

  • With 300 photos, 11.7 million parameters will memorize the training set.

  • Large steps on the pretrained layers, driven by a random head, can erase what made them useful.

Show answer

A. Dog photos look like ImageNet (which has many dog breeds), and 300 photos is small, so the frozen features are a strong, cheap start.

2After freezing every parameter of ResNet-18 and replacing fc with nn.Linear(512, 5), how many parameters are trainable?

  • That's the number of input features, not the number of weights.

  • 512 × 5 weights plus 5 biases.

  • That's the total; the frozen ones don't count as trainable.

Show answer

B. 512 × 5 weights plus 5 biases.

3A true box is (0, 0, 4, 4) and a predicted box is (2, 0, 6, 4). What is their IoU?

  • Half of each box overlaps, but the union is bigger than either box.

  • Overlap is 2 × 4 = 8. Union is 16 + 16 − 8 = 24. 8 / 24 = 1/3.

  • That's 8 / 32, the overlap divided by both areas added together. The union counts the shared area once, so it's 24.

Show answer

B. Overlap is 2 × 4 = 8. Union is 16 + 16 − 8 = 24. 8 / 24 = 1/3.

4A biology lab wants to count the cells in each microscope image and measure each one's area. Which output fits?

  • One label per image can't count or measure.

  • It labels every pixel "cell" or "background", so two touching cells merge into one blob.

  • Each cell gets its own mask, so you can count them and measure each one's area.

Show answer

C. Each cell gets its own mask, so you can count them and measure each one's area.

Key takeaways

  • A pretrained backbone has learned general visual features; replacing only the head lets a few hundred labels train a good classifier.
  • Freeze with requires_grad = False, replace model.fc, and pass only trainable parameters to the optimizer.
  • Unfreeze more as you get more data or as your images move away from everyday photos, with smaller learning rates for pretrained layers.
  • Detection returns boxes, labels, and scores; segmentation returns a class per pixel (semantic) or a mask per object (instance).
  • IoU measures overlap; NMS uses it to remove duplicate boxes for the same object.

#Further reading

  • CS231n: Transfer Learning (opens in a new tab): short notes on when to freeze and when to fine-tune, from the Stanford course.
  • torchvision: Models and pre-trained weights (opens in a new tab): every classification, detection, and segmentation model, with its weights enum and accuracy.
  • TorchVision Object Detection Finetuning Tutorial (opens in a new tab): fine-tuning Mask R-CNN on a small pedestrian dataset, the detection version of this lesson.

What you'll learn

  • Write train and evaluation transforms that match ImageNet-pretrained weights.
  • Freeze ResNet-18, attach a 102-class head, and keep BatchNorm statistics fixed.
  • Smoke-test a training loop on fake data by overfitting one small batch.
  • Unfreeze the last stage with a smaller learning rate and a cosine schedule.
  • Assemble the full two-phase script and run it on a Colab GPU.

Oxford Flowers-102 is a classic transfer-learning test: 102 species of flowers, but only 10 training images per species. That's 1,020 photos to learn 102 classes, some of which look almost identical. Trained from scratch, a network has far too little to go on. Starting from ImageNet weights, it doesn't need much.

Here's the plan:

Downloading the dataset and the weights needs Colab, but almost everything that can go wrong (a transform that produces the wrong shape, a loop that never updates the head, a learning rate set on the wrong layers) can be caught on any CPU in seconds. So you'll build each piece here, check it, and then run the finished script on a GPU.

#Step 1: Transforms that match the pretrained weights

ResNet-18's ImageNet weights expect 224×224 crops, scaled to 0–1, then normalized with ImageNet's per-channel mean and standard deviation. Training adds randomness on top; evaluation must be the same every time.

ToImage turns the NumPy array (height, width, channels) into a tensor image (channels, height, width). After normalizing, an average ImageNet pixel maps to 0 in every channel; this photo has a dark background, so its means come out below zero. Those are the units the first conv layer worked in during ImageNet training. Now look at what the model will receive. To display a normalized image you have to undo the normalization:

Every training view is still clearly the same flower, which is the test for any augmentation.

#Step 2: A fake dataset with the real interface

In Colab, the data comes from datasets.Flowers102("data", split="train", download=True, transform=train_tf), with matching "val" and "test" splits (1,020, 1,020, and 6,149 images). Each item is a (PIL image, label) pair.

datasets.FakeData returns random images in exactly that format, with no download. It's the perfect stand-in for checking the plumbing:

A batch of 16 normalized 224×224 images and integer labels: the same shapes the real loader will produce.

#Step 3: Freeze the backbone and attach the new head

Locally there are no pretrained weights, so WEIGHTS is None and the backbone is random. The structure, the shapes, and the parameter counts are identical, which is all these checks need.

52,326 trainable numbers (512 × 102 + 102), and two images in give two rows of 102 scores out.

#Step 4: A training loop that leaves BatchNorm alone

Recall the warning from the notes: in train() mode, BatchNorm layers keep updating their running statistics even when their weights are frozen. With 1,020 images and a small batch, those statistics would drift away from the ImageNet values the frozen layers depend on. train_epoch switches every BatchNorm layer back to eval mode after model.train():

Accuracy on random images means nothing, so how do you test a loop on fake data? Ask it to do the one thing any working loop can do: memorize a single small batch. If the loss doesn't fall toward zero, something is broken (the optimizer holds the wrong parameters, the labels are misaligned, or gradients aren't flowing). Small 64×64 images keep this fast:

The loss starts near ln(102) ≈ 4.6, which is what a model guessing uniformly over 102 classes scores, and falls fast as the head memorizes the batch. That's the behavior you want to see before moving on.

#Step 5: Phase two unfreezes layer4 with smaller steps

After the head has trained for a few epochs, its gradients are sensible, and it's safe to let the last stage adapt too. The pretrained layers get a learning rate ten times smaller than the head, and a cosine schedule lowers both smoothly to zero over the phase:

Phase two trains about 8.4 million parameters instead of 52 thousand, so it's slower and easier to overfit. That's why it comes second, runs at small learning rates, and stops at the epoch with the best validation accuracy.

#Step 6: The full script for Colab

Switch the runtime to a T4 GPU, paste this into one cell, and run it. The first run downloads the flower images (a few hundred MB) and the ResNet-18 weights (about 45 MB). If a download stops with a network error, run the cell again; finished files are reused. Loading Flowers-102 needs SciPy, which Colab already has.

Chance is 1 in 102, under 1%. Watch the head-only phase climb far above that within its first epochs, using features nobody trained on flowers, and note how much phase two adds on top. Write both numbers down; the practice set asks you to compare them with a from-scratch run.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does train_epoch call .eval() on every BatchNorm layer right after model.train()?

  • The new head is a single Linear layer; it has no dropout.

  • In train mode BatchNorm updates those statistics on every batch, even when its weights are frozen.

  • They can; that's exactly why the statistics would drift.

Show answer

B. In train mode BatchNorm updates those statistics on every batch, even when its weights are frozen.

2Why does eval_tf use Resize(256) and CenterCrop(224) instead of RandomResizedCrop?

  • Random crops at test time would make accuracy change from run to run and would shift the inputs away from what the model expects.

  • The speed difference is negligible; consistency is the point.

  • Any transform works on any dataset; the choice is about what each split should measure.

Show answer

A. Random crops at test time would make accuracy change from run to run and would shift the inputs away from what the model expects.

3The memorize-one-batch check ends with the loss near zero. What does that prove?

  • It says nothing about generalization; the images were random noise.

  • A loop that can't memorize 16 images has a bug; one that can is ready for real data.

  • This check ran with random weights on purpose.

Show answer

B. A loop that can't memorize 16 images has a bug; one that can is ready for real data.

Key takeaways

  • Match the preprocessing the weights were trained with: 224×224 crops, values scaled to 0–1, ImageNet mean and standard deviation.
  • Augment only what keeps the label true; for flowers, crops and flips are safe and hue shifts are not.
  • Test the whole pipeline on FakeData by memorizing one batch before spending GPU time on real data.
  • Keep BatchNorm in eval mode when fine-tuning on small data.
  • Train the head first, then unfreeze the last stage with a learning rate about ten times smaller, and keep the epoch with the best validation accuracy.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Swap in models.resnet50(weights=models.ResNet50_Weights.DEFAULT). Its fc takes 2,048 features instead of 512, and it's slower; is the gain worth the time?
  • Run the same script with weights=None and every layer trainable, to measure what the pretrained weights were worth on this dataset.
  • Collect 20 photos per class for a small task of your own (three kinds of leaves, five kinds of pasta) in folders, load them with datasets.ImageFolder, and reuse this script unchanged except for the head size.

#Further reading

  • PyTorch: Transfer Learning for Computer Vision (opens in a new tab): the official tutorial, comparing fine-tuning everything with training only the head.
  • torchvision Flowers102 (opens in a new tab): the dataset class used here, including its splits and requirements.
  • CS231n: Transfer Learning (opens in a new tab): when to fine-tune how much, with practical learning-rate advice.

m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pick a transfer strategy from the size and look of a dataset, and count what each strategy trains.
  • Keep BatchNorm statistics fixed and prove it with a test.
  • Implement IoU and greedy non-maximum suppression, and match torchvision's results exactly.
  • Choose segmentation metrics that don't hide small classes.
  • Run a fair transfer-versus-scratch experiment and explain its result.

#Warm-up: which strategy?

For each project, choose between training only a new head, fine-tuning the last stage, and fine-tuning everything, starting from ImageNet weights.

  1. 500 photos of four bird species from a backyard feeder camera.
  2. 20,000 labeled satellite tiles of farmland, 8 crop types.
  3. 150 microscope images of three kinds of cell, all grayscale.
Show solution
  1. Head only. Birds look like ImageNet photos (which include many bird species), and 500 images is small.
  2. Everything, with a small learning rate for the backbone. Satellite tiles look nothing like everyday photos, and 20,000 labels is enough to move every layer safely.
  3. Head first, then the last stage, with strong augmentation, and compare the two on validation. The images are unusual and the dataset is tiny, so it's a judgment call you settle by measuring. Grayscale images need three channels for an ImageNet model: repeat the single channel (v2.Grayscale(num_output_channels=3) does it).

Run this setup cell first; the exercises use it.

#Exercise 1: Count what each strategy trains

Write prepare(num_classes, unfreeze) that builds models.resnet18(weights=None), freezes everything, unfreezes the stages named in the list unfreeze (for example ["layer4"]), and replaces the head. Print the trainable count for a 5-class problem with [], ["layer4"], ["layer3", "layer4"], and every stage unfrozen.

Need a hint?

getattr(model, "layer4") returns the stage by name. The head must be replaced after freezing, or it gets frozen too.

Show solution

Unfreezing layer4 multiplies the trainable count by more than 3,000. The last stage holds most of ResNet-18's weights because it has the most channels (512), which is one more reason to unfreeze it last and gently.

#Exercise 2: Prove BatchNorm stays put

Show that model.bn1.running_mean changes after one forward pass in train() mode even though every parameter is frozen. Then write freeze_bn(model), which puts every BatchNorm2d layer in eval mode, and a unittest that passes only when the running mean is unchanged after a training-mode forward pass.

Need a hint?

Clone the buffer before the forward pass (model.bn1.running_mean.clone()), otherwise you'll compare the tensor with itself. Use random input such as torch.randn(4, 3, 64, 64).

Show solution

requires_grad controls gradients; train() and eval() control behavior. They're separate switches, and frozen fine-tuning needs both set correctly.

#Exercise 3: IoU from scratch

Write iou(a, b) for two boxes in (x1, y1, x2, y2) form using plain Python arithmetic. Boxes that don't overlap must give exactly 0, not a negative number. Test it against torchvision.ops.box_iou on 200 random pairs.

Need a hint?

The overlap's left edge is the larger of the two left edges, and its right edge is the smaller of the two right edges. If right < left, the width is 0: use max(0, right - left).

Show solution

Without the max(0.0, ...), two boxes far apart in both directions give a negative width times a negative height, a positive "overlap", and a nonsense IoU.

#Exercise 4: Non-maximum suppression from scratch

Implement greedy NMS: sort boxes by score, highest first; keep the top box; drop every remaining box whose IoU with it is above the threshold; repeat on what's left. Return the kept indices in the order kept. Compare with torchvision.ops.nms on 40 random boxes for thresholds 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7.

Need a hint?

Keep a list remaining of indices sorted by score. Each round, pop the first one into kept, then rebuild remaining with only the boxes whose iou with it is at or below the threshold. Your counts will differ from the sample if your random boxes differ.

Show solution

A lower threshold suppresses more aggressively. That's a real trade-off: in a crowd, two people can overlap by more than 0.3, and a strict threshold would delete one of them.

#Exercise 5: A metric that hides the pedestrian

Here's a 12×12 street scene mask: 0 is background, 1 is road, 2 is a small pedestrian. The prediction gets the road nearly right but labels the pedestrian as road. Compute pixel accuracy (fraction of pixels correct) and IoU for each class, then the mean IoU over the three classes. Plot the two masks side by side.

Need a hint?

For class c, IoU is ((pred == c) & (truth == c)).sum() / ((pred == c) | (truth == c)).sum(). Pixel accuracy is (pred == truth).float().mean().

Show solution

Pixel accuracy rewards getting the big classes right, and the pedestrian is only 8 of 144 pixels. Per-class IoU puts every class on an equal footing, so the miss shows up as a 0 that drags the mean down. For anything safety-related, report the per-class numbers, not only the average.

#Exercise 6: When transfer learning loses

Test the transfer bet on the digits. Pretrain the small CNN from Module 5 on digits 0–4, then use its conv layers as a backbone for digits 5–9, with only k labeled images per class (try k = 3 and k = 10). Compare three strategies on a held-out set of 5–9: training from scratch, frozen backbone with a new head, and fine-tuning everything (backbone at 1e-4, head at 1e-3). Average two random draws of the labeled images. Does transfer help? Why or why not?

Need a hint?

Relabel 5–9 as 0–4 with y - 5 so a 5-output head works. Pick k images per class with a seeded torch.Generator. Train each target model for about 100 epochs on its handful of images, and copy the pretrained backbone with copy.deepcopy so runs don't share weights.

Show solution

Here transfer loses: training from scratch beats both transfer strategies at both label counts. That's not a bug. Transfer pays off when three things hold, and this setup breaks all of them:

  • The source is much bigger and more varied than the target. Here it's 900 small images of five digits; ImageNet is 1.28 million photos of 1,000 kinds of things.
  • The model is big enough to overfit a small target from scratch. This CNN has about 6,000 parameters, so 15 images don't let it memorize much. ResNet-18 has 11.7 million.
  • The target is hard. Telling 5–9 apart at 8×8 is easy enough that a few examples go a long way.

So measure, don't assume: a from-scratch baseline is the control every transfer-learning result needs.

#Challenge: precision and recall for one image

A detector returned these boxes for an image with three true objects:

Match predictions to true boxes greedily by score: each prediction, highest score first, claims the unmatched true box it overlaps most, if that IoU is at least 0.5. A matched prediction is a true positive; an unmatched one is a false positive (including a second box on an already-claimed object); an unclaimed true box is a false negative. Report precision, recall, and which mistake each false positive represents. Then repeat at IoU 0.3, and explain why the answer changes.

Need a hint?

Track claimed = set() of true-box indices. For each prediction, compute its IoU with every true box not in claimed and take the best. At IoU 0.5 you should find three different kinds of false positive: a duplicate, a box on empty background, and a box in roughly the right place that isn't tight enough. Your iou from Exercise 3 does all the geometry.
