What you'll learn

  • List what a run record needs so someone else can reproduce a result, and log it to CSV.
  • Show that a fixed seed reproduces a run exactly, and know where GPUs break that promise.
  • Estimate training memory from parameters, gradients, optimizer state, and activations.
  • Explain what mixed precision changes and why float16 needs a gradient scaler.
  • Evaluate beyond accuracy: per-class errors, failure galleries, and subgroup results.

Two weeks ago a teammate posted "97.8% on the test set!" in the project chat. Today nobody can get above 95%. Was it a different seed? A different split? A learning rate someone changed and changed back? The notebook has been edited since, and the cell that printed 97.8% no longer exists.

Even if the number were reproducible, it would leave out two things a reader needs: what the run cost (time, GPU memory), and who the remaining 2.2% of errors land on. This lesson covers all three: recording runs, budgeting resources, and evaluating for real.

#What a run record needs

A result is reproducible when someone else can rerun it from your record alone. That takes six things:

Record Example Why
Config learning rate, batch size, epochs, augmentation Every choice that changes the result
Seeds seed=0 for weights, batch order, augmentation Randomness is part of the run
Data dataset version and the exact split (seed or index file) A different split is a different experiment
Code the git commit hash The code changes more often than you think
Environment torch and torchvision versions, GPU name Defaults and kernels change between versions
Results per-epoch metrics, final metrics, time, peak memory The curve, not just the last number

Start with seeds. Here's a tiny training run on the digits, run three times:

The same seed gives bit-for-bit the same numbers, and changing only the seed moves the result. That second fact matters as much as the first: if seed 1 scores lower than seed 0, a 0.5-point "improvement" from a new idea may just be noise. Run important comparisons with three or more seeds and report the spread.

📝 Note

On a GPU, the same seed can still give slightly different numbers, because some CUDA kernels add floating-point values in a nondeterministic order. torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) forces deterministic versions (and raises an error for operations that have none), and torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False stops cuDNN from picking different algorithms between runs. Both can cost speed.

#Logging every run to one file

A CSV file with one row per epoch per run is a perfectly good experiment tracker. Each row carries the run's id and config, so you can filter and plot later; a JSON file next to it holds the environment.

TensorBoard does the same job with live charts. In Colab, SummaryWriter writes event files under runs/, and the notebook commands %load_ext tensorboard and %tensorboard --logdir runs open the dashboard inside the notebook. Colab has TensorBoard installed; on a machine without it, the import below fails with an error until you install the tensorboard package.

Pick one tool and use it for every run, including the ones that fail. The failed runs are what tell you which ideas you've already tried.

#Where GPU memory goes

During training with Adam in float32, GPU memory holds four things:

  • Weights: 4 bytes per parameter.
  • Gradients: another 4 bytes per parameter.
  • Adam's state: two running averages per parameter, 8 more bytes.
  • Activations: every layer's output, saved for the backward pass. This part grows with batch size and image size.

The first three are fixed: 16 bytes per parameter. The fourth is the one you control. You can estimate it on a CPU by adding up the size of every layer's output for one image:

For ResNet-18 the fixed part is under 0.2 GB; activations are nearly everything. Doubling the batch size doubles activation memory. Doubling the image's width and height multiplies it by four, because every feature map has four times as many pixels. When a batch doesn't fit, PyTorch stops with torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate .... The usual fixes, in order: halve the batch size, turn on mixed precision, or keep the batch size and use gradient accumulation (call backward() on several small batches and step() once).

Measure instead of guessing once you're on the GPU. On a CPU runtime these calls raise an error, because there is no CUDA device:

#Mixed precision: half the bytes, with a safety net

float16 stores a number in 2 bytes instead of float32's 4. That halves activation memory, and GPUs like the T4 have tensor cores that multiply float16 matrices much faster than float32 ones. The catch is range: float16 can't represent numbers smaller than about 6 × 10⁻⁸, and small gradients are often that small.

That's exactly what a gradient scaler does: multiply the loss by a large factor so gradients survive in float16, then divide them back before the optimizer step (and skip the step if anything overflowed). Autocast decides which operations run in float16 (matrix multiplications and convolutions) and which stay in float32 (sums, softmax, losses). In a training loop on a GPU it looks like the code below; without a CUDA device and the rest of the loop defined, it stops with an error.

Newer GPUs also support bfloat16, which keeps float32's range with less precision and usually doesn't need a scaler. The T4 doesn't have fast bfloat16, so on free Colab use float16 with the scaler.

#One accuracy number hides who the errors land on

In 2018, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested three commercial gender-classification systems, from Microsoft, Face++, and IBM, on 1,270 photos of parliament members, labeled by gender and by skin type. Their paper, Gender Shades, reported overall error rates of 6.3%, 10.0%, and 12.1%. Then they split the errors by subgroup:

Every system did worst on darker-skinned women, with error rates up to 34.7%. For lighter-skinned men, no system's error rate was above 0.8%. Three lessons carry over to any vision model:

  1. Slice the test set. Report results per class and per subgroup, not only overall. The overall numbers above look acceptable; the slices don't.
  2. Slice by combinations. Microsoft's error on women overall was 10.7% and on darker-skinned people overall 12.9%, but on darker-skinned women it was 20.8%. Single-attribute slices can hide the worst-served group.
  3. Check what you trained and tested on. The paper found that two widely used face benchmarks were 79.6% and 86.2% lighter-skinned. A benchmark that underrepresents a group can't reveal how badly a model serves it.

For your own models, the same practice applies with whatever metadata you have: camera type, lighting, location, image size, the kind of document or the hospital a scan came from. Two more tools complete the picture: a confusion matrix, which shows which classes get mistaken for which, and a failure gallery, a grid of the actual misclassified images with their true and predicted labels. You'll build both in the next lesson.

⚠️ Watch out

total_loss += loss leaks memory. loss is a tensor that still holds its computation graph, so adding it to a running total keeps every batch's graph alive, and memory grows until the run dies with an out-of-memory error. Use total_loss += loss.item(), which copies out a plain Python number.

⚠️ Watch out

Don't report your luckiest run. Training ten seeds and quoting the best test score is selecting on the test set. Choose settings on validation data, then report the test result as a mean and spread across seeds.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model has 25 million parameters and trains with Adam in float32. Roughly how much memory do weights, gradients, and optimizer state take, before activations?

  • That's only the weights (25 million × 4 bytes).

  • Weights plus gradients; Adam adds two more values per parameter.

  • 4 + 4 + 8 = 16 bytes per parameter, times 25 million.

Show answer

C. 4 + 4 + 8 = 16 bytes per parameter, times 25 million.

2Batch size 256 runs out of GPU memory, but you want the training to behave like batch 256. What do you change?

  • The learning rate doesn't change memory use.

  • Activations scale with the micro-batch size, and the summed gradients act like one batch of 256.

  • More epochs reuse the same memory per step; it still won't fit.

Show answer

B. Activations scale with the micro-batch size, and the summed gradients act like one batch of 256.

3Why does float16 training use a gradient scaler?

  • It can; it has a sign bit like float32.

  • The scaler moves gradients into float16's representable range and back.

  • It's about not losing gradients, not about speed of convergence.

Show answer

B. The scaler moves gradients into float16's representable range and back.

4A model's overall error is 6%. Error is 1% for one subgroup and 21% for another. What's the most useful next step?

  • The average is the number that hides the problem.

  • Disaggregated results are the finding; representation is the first place to look for a cause.

  • That hides the failure instead of fixing it.

Show answer

B. Disaggregated results are the finding; representation is the first place to look for a cause.

Key takeaways

  • A reproducible result comes with its config, seeds, data split, code version, environment, and per-epoch metrics.
  • The same seed reproduces a CPU run exactly; compare ideas across several seeds, because seed-to-seed noise is real.
  • Training memory is about 16 bytes per parameter with Adam, plus activations that grow with batch and image size.
  • Mixed precision halves activation memory and speeds up matrix math; float16 needs autocast and a gradient scaler.
  • Evaluate per class and per subgroup, including combinations of attributes; overall accuracy can hide large failures.

#Further reading

  • Gender Shades (Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018) (opens in a new tab): the paper, short and readable, with the full subgroup tables.
  • PyTorch: Reproducibility (opens in a new tab): every source of randomness in PyTorch, and how to control each one.
  • PyTorch: Automatic Mixed Precision (opens in a new tab): which operations autocast runs in float16, and how GradScaler works.

What you'll learn

  • Write run_experiment(config) that seeds, trains, times, and logs every epoch to a shared CSV file.
  • Sweep a small grid of settings, plot the logged curves, and choose a winner on validation data.
  • Evaluate the winner once on the test set with a confusion matrix and per-class precision and recall.
  • Build a failure gallery of the model's most confident mistakes.
  • Compare accuracy across a metadata subgroup, with sample sizes and 95% intervals.

The goal is a short, honest report on a digit classifier: what was tried, which run won and why, what it costs to run, and where it fails. Here's the pipeline:

#Step 1: Data with a metadata column

Real datasets come with metadata: which camera, which clinic, which day. The digits don't, so we'll simulate one realistic kind. Suppose most of the forms were scanned on scanner A, but about one in eight went through an older scanner B that blurs and fades the ink. We pass a random 12% of the images through a blur-and-fade function and record which scanner each image came from.

The split was stratified by digit, not by scanner, so each split has roughly the same share of scanner B, as you'd expect from a random split.

#Step 2: An experiment runner that logs as it goes

run_experiment takes a config dictionary and does everything a reproducible run needs: seed first, build, train, measure validation accuracy and time per epoch, and append one row per epoch to runs.csv. The config is saved next to it as JSON with the library versions.

Notice loss.item() in the running total, not loss: the warning from the notes about leaking computation graphs applies to every loop you write.

#Step 3: Sweep four configurations and read the log

Two learning rates, with and without shift augmentation. Every run uses the same seed, so the only differences are the settings.

The log is plain data, so plotting every run is a few lines of pandas and matplotlib:

The validation set looks like the training data (mostly centered digits), so augmentation for shifts doesn't pay off here; it would if the validation data contained shifted digits. The winner is the run with the best final validation accuracy. We pick it before looking at the test set.

#Step 4: Test once, with a confusion matrix

The matrix tells you which mistakes happen, which accuracy can't: here the most common one is an 8 read as a 1, and 8 has the lowest recall. In the report, recall for a digit is the share of that digit's images the model got right, and precision is the share of that digit's predictions that were correct. A digit with low recall is being missed; one with low precision is being guessed when it isn't there.

#Step 5: A gallery of the most confident mistakes

Numbers summarize failures; pictures explain them. Sort the mistakes by how confident the model was, and look at them:

Look for patterns a person can name: a particular pair of digits, unusual handwriting, or a recording condition. Here, three of the twelve are 8s read as 1s; at 8×8 pixels, a narrow 8 whose loops fill in looks like one thick stroke. Only one of the twelve came from scanner B, a first hint that any scanner gap is small.

#Step 6: Accuracy by subgroup, with intervals

The gallery suggests a hypothesis; the subgroup table tests it. With small groups, a bare percentage is misleading, so each row gets a 95% Wilson interval, a standard confidence interval for a proportion that behaves well with small counts:

Scanner B's measured accuracy is lower, but look at the intervals. B's runs from about 81% to 97% and overlaps A's, because it rests on only 50 images. This test set can't tell a real gap from bad luck, and the report should say exactly that: B may be worse, and the evidence is thin. The next step is more scanner-B test images; a few hundred would narrow its interval to a few points. Compare Gender Shades, where each subgroup had hundreds of faces and the gaps were many times larger than the noise.

#Step 7: Write the report

The last step turns all of this into a file someone else can read without running anything:

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the code choose the winning configuration before computing any test metric?

  • The test set is only an unbiased estimate if nothing was chosen by looking at it.

  • It's the same size as validation; the reason is about bias, not size.

  • The CSV could hold anything; the choice is deliberate.

Show answer

A. The test set is only an unbiased estimate if nothing was chosen by looking at it.

2Scanner B scored 92% with a 95% interval of about 81% to 97%; scanner A scored 96.5% (94% to 98%). What can the report claim?

  • The intervals overlap, so this test set can't rule out that the gap is luck.

  • The honest claim names the difference, the sample size, and the uncertainty, and asks for more B data.

  • Overlapping intervals don't show equality either; a real gap of several points is still quite possible.

Show answer

B. The honest claim names the difference, the sample size, and the uncertainty, and asks for more B data.

3Why does each CSV row repeat the full config instead of just the run id?

  • Empty cells are allowed; the repetition is a choice.

  • log[log.lr == 0.003] just works.

  • Size isn't a goal.

Show answer

B. log[log.lr == 0.003] just works.

Key takeaways

  • One runner function that seeds, trains, times, and logs every epoch makes every run comparable and reproducible.
  • Read the log back as data: plot all the curves and summarize every run, then choose the winner on validation.
  • A confusion matrix shows which classes get confused; precision and recall per class show missing versus over-guessing.
  • A failure gallery turns error counts into patterns you can name.
  • Report subgroup accuracy with its sample size and interval; small groups need more data before their numbers mean much.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Run each configuration with three seeds and plot the mean with a shaded band for the spread.
  • Add a val_shift_acc column (validation accuracy on shifted digits) and see whether the augmented runs win when it's part of the selection rule.
  • Add scanner-B augmentation (blur plus fade) to training and rerun the audit. Does the gap close, and what happens to scanner A?
  • Swap the CSV for TensorBoard in Colab: one SummaryWriter per run, with add_scalar in place of writer.writerow.

#Further reading

  • A Recipe for Training Neural Networks (Karpathy) (opens in a new tab): how an experienced practitioner sets up, logs, and debugs training runs.
  • scikit-learn: Metrics and scoring (opens in a new tab): precision, recall, confusion matrices, and every other classification metric, with definitions.
  • How to use TensorBoard with PyTorch (opens in a new tab): the official recipe for logging scalars and opening the dashboard.

What you'll learn

  • Turn a parameter count into a training-memory estimate for different optimizers.
  • Pick the largest batch size that fits a GPU, and see how image size changes it.
  • Prove that gradient accumulation reproduces a larger batch's gradient.
  • Write a test that catches randomness torch.manual_seed doesn't control.
  • Compute per-class precision and recall from a confusion matrix, and size a subgroup test set.

#Warm-up: memory in your head

A model has 60 million parameters and trains in float32. How much memory do the weights, gradients, and optimizer state need with Adam? With plain SGD and no momentum?

Show solution

Adam: 4 (weights) + 4 (gradients) + 8 (two running averages) = 16 bytes per parameter, so 60M × 16 = 960 MB. Plain SGD keeps no extra state: 8 bytes per parameter, 480 MB. SGD with momentum keeps one running average: 12 bytes, 720 MB. Activations come on top of all three.

Run the setup cell first:

#Exercise 1: A memory estimator

Write training_memory_mb(model, optimizer) that returns the megabytes (10⁶ bytes) needed for weights, gradients, and optimizer state in float32, for "sgd", "momentum", and "adam". Count only parameters with requires_grad=True for gradients and optimizer state, since frozen layers need neither. Print a table for ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 (with weights=None), plus ResNet-50 with everything frozen except a new 10-class head.

Need a hint?

Weights always cost 4 bytes per parameter. Gradients cost 4 per trainable parameter. Momentum adds 4 per trainable parameter and Adam adds 8.

Show solution

With only the head trainable, the optimizer barely matters: almost all of the memory is the frozen weights themselves. That's one more reason feature extraction is cheap.

#Exercise 2: The largest batch that fits

For ResNet-18 trained with Adam, estimate the per-image activation memory at 224×224 and at 128×128 (sum every leaf layer's output size, as in the notes). With a 15 GB GPU and 20% kept free as headroom, what is the largest power-of-two batch size at each resolution?

Need a hint?

Usable memory is 15 × 0.8 = 12 GB. Subtract the fixed cost from Exercise 1, divide by the per-image cost, and round down to a power of two with 2 ** int(np.log2(n)). Use a fresh model for each measurement so old hooks don't add up.

Show solution

Shrinking images from 224 to 128 cuts the pixels per feature map by about two thirds, so about three times as many images fit. This is only an estimate; confirm with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() on the real GPU before a long run.

#Exercise 3: Gradient accumulation really matches the big batch

Take nn.Linear(64, 10) and 64 digit images. Compute the gradient of the mean cross-entropy loss on all 64 at once. Then zero the gradients and accumulate over four micro-batches of 16, calling backward() on each micro-batch's loss divided by 4. Write a unittest that checks the two gradients match with torch.allclose, and a second test showing that forgetting the division gives gradients four times too large.

Need a hint?

backward() adds into .grad; it doesn't overwrite. The mean over 64 equals the average of the four means over 16, which is why each micro-batch loss is divided by the number of micro-batches.

Show solution

The bug in the second test doesn't crash anything; it just behaves like a learning rate four times too high. One caveat: accumulation matches a big batch exactly only for models without BatchNorm, whose statistics are computed per micro-batch.

#Exercise 4: The seed that didn't seed

This augmentation uses Python's random module to decide whether to add noise. Write a test that trains twice with torch.manual_seed(0) and checks the final weights are identical. Run it, explain why it fails, and fix noisy so the test passes.

Need a hint?

torch.manual_seed seeds PyTorch's generators only. Python's random and NumPy each have their own. Either seed them too, or draw the coin flip with torch.rand(1).item().

Show solution

Python's random kept advancing between the two training runs, so the coin flips differed and so did the noise. Libraries you call can hide the same problem, which is why a "same seed, same weights" test belongs in every project.

#Exercise 5: Read a confusion matrix

A wildlife-camera classifier for four animals produced this confusion matrix on its test set (rows are the true class, columns the prediction):

Compute overall accuracy, then precision and recall for every class. Which pair of classes gets confused most, and in which direction? Which class would you collect more data for first?

Need a hint?

Recall for class i is cm[i, i] / cm[i].sum() (the row). Precision is cm[i, i] / cm[:, i].sum() (the column). For the most confused pair, zero the diagonal and find the largest remaining cell with np.unravel_index(off.argmax(), off.shape).

Show solution

Foxes are called coyotes 52 times, while coyotes are called foxes only 20 times, so the confusion is lopsided, and fox has the lowest recall. Wolf is close behind: a quarter of the wolves are missed, again mostly as coyotes, and wolf is the rarest class with only 100 test images. Coyote's low precision is the other side of the same coin, since it soaks up foxes and wolves. More fox and coyote photos in similar poses and lighting, and more wolves overall, are the first data to collect.

#Exercise 6: How many images does a subgroup need?

A street-sign detector scores 95.1% on 900 daytime test images and 85.0% on 60 nighttime ones. Compute 95% Wilson intervals for both. Then find the smallest number of night images for which the night interval would be at most ±3 points wide, assuming accuracy stays at 85%.

Need a hint?

Reuse the wilson function from the build-along. Loop n upward from 60 until (high - low) / 2 <= 0.03. The number of correct images is round(0.85 * n).

Show solution

Here the intervals don't overlap, so the night gap is real even with 60 images. But "somewhere between 74% and 92%" is too vague to set a safety threshold with; you need several hundred night images to pin it down to a few points. Plan subgroup test sets by the precision you need, not by their share of the data.

#Challenge: is the model's confidence honest?

Train a small classifier on the digits (any model from this course), and for every test prediction record the top probability and whether it was right. Split predictions into 10 bins by confidence (0.0–0.1, …, 0.9–1.0). In each bin, compare the average confidence with the actual accuracy, plot the two against each other (a reliability diagram), and compute the expected calibration error: the average gap between confidence and accuracy across bins, weighted by how many predictions fall in each bin. Is your model overconfident or underconfident?

Need a hint?

np.digitize(conf, np.linspace(0, 1, 11)[1:-1]) assigns each prediction a bin from 0 to 9. Skip empty bins. A perfectly calibrated model's points lie on the diagonal line from (0, 0) to (1, 1); points below it mean the model is more confident than it is accurate.

What you'll learn

  • Explain what the capstone asks for and how each part maps to Modules 2 to 7.
  • Choose a project whose data, compute, and risks you can handle in the time you have.
  • Document a dataset with the questions a datasheet asks.
  • Write a one-page plan with a baseline, a metric chosen in advance, subgroups, and a compute budget.

A model study isn't a leaderboard entry. Anyone can post "94% accuracy." Your study answers the questions a careful reader asks next: 94% on what data, compared with what baseline, at what cost, failing on which images, and safe to use for what? This page is the brief and the planning; the next two lessons cover building and presenting.

#What you'll hand in

  1. A notebook that trains and evaluates a vision model from start to finish, and reruns from top to bottom without errors.
  2. An experiment log (runs.csv or TensorBoard) with at least three runs, including a simple baseline.
  3. A model card, one to two pages, describing the model, its data, its results by subgroup, and where it should and shouldn't be used.
  4. A five-minute presentation of the question, the evidence, and the limits.

Every requirement is something you've already practiced:

Requirement Where you learned it
Datasheet: source, license, size, splits, who and what is represented This lesson
Architecture and why you chose it, with tensor shapes traced Modules 2 and 5
Training loop with a validation curve, seeded and logged Modules 4 and 7
Augmentation chosen to keep labels true, and shown on real examples Module 5
Transfer learning or a justified decision not to use it Module 6
Metrics: overall, per class, and at least one subgroup or condition with intervals Module 7
A failure gallery and a written diagnosis of the patterns Module 7
Resources: training time, hardware, parameters, peak memory Module 7
Model card with intended use, out-of-scope uses, and limitations Lessons 2 and 3 of this module

#Five project ideas

Pick one, or propose your own at the same scale. The level describes the data and compute, not the thinking; every option needs the same careful evaluation.

1. Scanner robustness for digit reading (starter level; runs on any CPU). Use load_digits and simulate two or three recording conditions (blur, fading, shifts, low resolution). Study which conditions break a CNN, which augmentations fix which failures, and what each fix costs on clean images. The next lesson's starter code is built on this project.

2. Augmentation study on CIFAR-10 (intermediate; Colab GPU). 60,000 small color photos in 10 classes. Train a small CNN with no augmentation, then add crops, flips, and color jitter one at a time. Which help, which hurt, and which classes benefit? Cats and dogs are the classic confusion; does augmentation help them, or only the easy classes?

3. Flowers with ten labels per class (intermediate; Colab GPU). Oxford Flowers-102 has exactly ten training images per species. Compare training from scratch, a frozen ResNet-18 with a new head, and fine-tuning the last stage, at 2, 5, and 10 images per class. Plot the learning curve for each, and find the species the best model still confuses.

4. Your own small dataset (advanced; Colab GPU). Photograph 30 to 50 examples per class of something local: recycling categories, leaf types, lab glassware. Load them with datasets.ImageFolder and use transfer learning. The challenge is documentation: record where, when, and how you photographed, then test on images taken in different conditions (a different room, a phone, daylight versus lamp light) to measure what your collection process baked in. Don't photograph people.

5. Audit a pretrained pedestrian detector (advanced; Colab GPU). The Penn-Fudan dataset has 170 street images with 345 labeled pedestrians, and it's used in the official torchvision detection tutorial. Run a COCO-pretrained Faster R-CNN on it, match detections to labels at IoU 0.5, and report recall by person size (small, medium, large boxes) and by how occluded each person is. You're evaluating, not training, so the work is in the matching code and the failure gallery.

⚠️ Watch out

Some vision tasks are out of scope for this capstone, however interesting they look: classifying people's gender, race, age, emotion, or identity from their faces, or any model that judges people from photos. Gender Shades showed how these systems fail unequally; building one well needs consent, careful labeling, and an ethics review you can't do in a course project. Project 5 involves people in public street photos, but it measures whether a safety-relevant detector finds everyone; it doesn't label who they are.

#Document the dataset before you train

Researchers call this a datasheet, after Gebru and colleagues' paper Datasheets for Datasets. For a course project, answer these in a few sentences each:

  • Motivation: who made this dataset, and for what task?
  • Composition: how many images, how many per class, what resolution? What's in the images besides the label (backgrounds, people, text)?
  • Collection: how were images gathered and labeled? Who labeled them, and how do you know the labels are right? Look at 50 random images with their labels and count the mistakes.
  • Coverage: which conditions, places, or groups are represented, and which are missing? This is where your subgroup slices come from.
  • License and use: may you use it for this? Cite it the way its authors ask.
  • Splits: how are train, validation, and test separated? Could near-duplicate images (the same object photographed twice, the same writer, the same video) end up on both sides?

The last question catches the most common hidden flaw in vision projects. If two photos of the same leaf land in train and test, the test score measures memory, not generalization.

#Fill in the plan

Copy this template into the first text cell of your notebook and fill it in before writing training code. Writing the metric and the subgroups down first is what keeps you from choosing them after you've seen which ones look good.

The compute budget deserves real numbers. Time one epoch of your baseline, multiply by epochs and by the number of runs (three seeds each for the runs you'll compare), and add a margin. Colab's free tier can disconnect long sessions, so plan runs of under an hour, save checkpoints and runs.csv to Google Drive as you go, and make every cell safe to rerun.

#Five milestones

Milestone Done when
M1 Data Datasheet answered, splits fixed and saved, 20 random examples plotted with labels, duplicate check run
M2 Baseline Baseline trained with a fixed seed, curves logged, validation score recorded
M3 Experiments Each change run against the baseline with the same seeds, all runs in the log
M4 Evaluation Best run chosen on validation, test evaluated once: per-class table, confusion matrix, subgroup table with intervals, failure gallery
M5 Communication Model card written, tests passing, notebook reruns cleanly, five-minute talk rehearsed

Give M4 as much time as M2 and M3 together. Training is the part that feels like progress, but the evaluation is where the study earns its conclusions.

💡 Tip

Pick the project you can finish. A small dataset studied carefully, with honest subgroup results and a clear limitations section, is a stronger capstone than a large model with one accuracy number.

  • Generate a model card from the results instead of retyping numbers.

This lesson is a complete, working version of project 1 from the brief: a digit reader that will face scanned forms in three conditions it never saw in training (shifted, faded, and blurred). The study's question is: which augmentation makes a digit CNN robust to these conditions, and what does it cost on clean images?

Every section below is one milestone. If you chose a different project, run this once to see the whole shape, then replace the parts marked in the last section. The code is short on purpose; your project's version will grow, but the structure should stay this simple.

#Milestone 1: Config, data, and the datasheet

All settings live in one dataclass, so a run is fully described by one object you can log.

The duplicate check compares the exact pixels of every training image against every test image. Zero here; on your own photos, also look for near-duplicates (bursts of the same shot) by eye or with a perceptual hash. Next, the habit that catches label and loading bugs early: plot random examples with their labels, under every condition.

#Milestone 2: A logged, seeded baseline

The runner is the one from Module 7, trimmed: seed, build, train, and append each epoch to runs.csv. Validation accuracy is recorded under every condition, because the deployment will see all of them.

The baseline does well on clean validation images and much worse under the conditions it never trained on. That gap is the study's starting point, and it's on record before any experiment runs.

#Milestone 3: Experiments against the baseline, with seeds

Each experiment changes one thing: the augmentation. Every configuration runs with two seeds (use three or more in your project if time allows), so you can see how much of a difference is just noise.

The table's last columns are the spread across seeds and the training time. A difference between two augmentations that's smaller than their seed-to-seed spread isn't a finding yet.

#Milestone 4: Choose on validation, test once, and audit

The plan fixed the primary metric in advance: mean validation accuracy across the four conditions. The winner is chosen by that number alone, then the test set is used once.

Read the table row by row. The chosen model gains a lot on shifted digits and a little on blurred ones, matches the baseline on faded ones, and gives up about eight points on clean images. Its margin over the baseline in mean validation accuracy was about the size of the seed-to-seed spread, so the honest summary is a trade-off, not a clear win. That's a normal outcome for a first round, and it tells you the next experiment: the augmented model has a harder training task and may simply need more epochs or a wider network.

Now the failure gallery for the chosen model, under its weakest condition:

Write down what you see in plain words before moving on; that sentence goes straight into the model card's limitations.

#Milestone 5: Generate the model card

Typing numbers into a document by hand is how reports drift away from results. Generate the card from the variables instead, then edit the prose around them:

Part Project 1 (this page) What to change for yours

Conditions or subgroups Simulated shift, fade, blur Metadata you recorded (lighting, location, camera) or object size for detection

Keep the order of the milestones even when the code changes. In particular, don't skip ahead to Milestone 4's test evaluation "just to see"; once you've seen test numbers, every later choice is tainted by them.

💡 Tip

In Colab, write runs.csv, checkpoints, and MODEL_CARD.md into a folder on Google Drive (mount it from the Files panel) so a disconnected session doesn't erase your log.

What you'll learn

  • Write automated tests for shapes, data splits, augmentation, learning, determinism, and evaluation side effects.
  • Polish a notebook so it reruns from a fresh runtime and every number in the write-up comes from code.
  • Write a model card whose limitations are specific enough to act on.
  • Present the study in five minutes and assess it with the rubric.

A study is finished when someone who wasn't there can trust it. That takes three things beyond the results: tests that show the pipeline does what you say it does, a model card that says what the model is for and where it breaks, and a short talk that puts the evidence before the conclusions.

#Six tests every vision project should have

Each test below targets a bug that silently ruins vision projects, the kind that produces a plausible number instead of a crash. They're written against a compact version of the capstone starter; in your project, point them at your own functions.

What each test protects against:

  1. Output shape: a wrong Linear size, or a flatten that merges the batch dimension.
  2. Disjoint splits: leakage from splitting twice with different seeds, or the same photo saved under two names.
  3. Augmentation range: a transform that pushes pixel values outside what the model trained on, or silently changes the dtype.
  4. Overfit one batch: a loop that doesn't learn (optimizer holding the wrong parameters, labels shuffled separately from images, a missing zero_grad).
  5. Determinism: randomness that torch.manual_seed doesn't control, which makes every comparison between runs unreliable.
  6. Evaluation side effects: evaluating in training mode (BatchNorm statistics change, dropout stays on) or accidentally taking an optimizer step.

Run them after every significant change. In your presentation, "all six tests pass" is a sentence that earns trust.

#Polish the notebook

Before you call it done:

  • Restart and run all (Runtime › Restart session and run all in Colab). Fix anything that depended on a cell you deleted or ran out of order.
  • Generate every number. Tables, the model card, and slide figures come from code, never retyped. If a number appears in your talk, you should be able to point to the cell that made it.
  • Print the environment at the top: torch and torchvision versions, GPU name, and the date.
  • Label every chart with a title, axis labels, and units, and say in a sentence what to notice.
  • Delete dead ends from the notebook, but keep them in the log. A failed run is evidence; a stale cell is a trap.

#Write a model card that's specific

The model card is the part people will read without opening your notebook. Use these sections, which follow Mitchell and colleagues' Model Cards for Model Reporting:

Most model cards fail at limitations, by being vague. Compare:

Vague Specific
"May not work in all conditions." "Accuracy on digits shifted one pixel diagonally is 62% (95% interval 57–67%), versus 89% on clean digits."
"The dataset may be biased." "All training photos were taken indoors under ceiling lights; outdoor accuracy was not measured."
"Results could vary." "The augmented and baseline models differ by less than their seed-to-seed spread on mean validation accuracy."

A specific limitation tells a reader exactly what to test before trusting the model in their setting.

#Present it in five minutes

  • Lead with the question, not the architecture. "Can a digit reader trained on clean scans handle faded ones?" beats "I used a two-layer CNN."
  • Show examples early. Six images from your dataset explain it faster than a paragraph.
  • One main result per slide, with the baseline beside it and the interval visible.
  • Show three failures from your gallery and say what pattern they share.
  • End with a limitation and a next step, not with your best number.

Rehearse with a timer. Five minutes is about 650 spoken words.

#The rubric

Criterion Points Strong Developing
Question and plan 10 One clear question; metric and subgroups fixed before training Question vague, or metric chosen after results
Data and datasheet 15 Source, license, splits, coverage gaps, and a duplicate check documented Dataset named but not described; leakage not checked
Experiments 20 Logged baseline; one change at a time; at least two seeds for compared runs Runs not logged, several changes at once, single seed
Evaluation 25 Test used once; per-class and subgroup results with intervals; failure gallery with a named pattern Only overall accuracy; test reused for choices
Resources and reproducibility 10 Time, hardware, parameters, peak memory; tests pass; reruns cleanly Missing costs; notebook only runs in a certain order
Model card 10 Intended and out-of-scope uses; specific, measured limitations Generic limitations, or missing
Presentation 10 Under five minutes; evidence before claims; failures shown Over time; claims without the numbers behind them

A study with modest accuracy and excellent evaluation will score well. A high accuracy number with no baseline, no seeds, and no subgroup results won't.

#Reflect before you move on

Write a short paragraph answering each:

  1. Which result surprised you, and what does that say about the assumption you started with?
  2. Which subgroup or condition would you most want more test data for, and roughly how many images would make its interval useful?
  3. If someone used your model outside its intended use tomorrow, what's the most likely way it would fail, and who would notice?
  4. What would you do with ten times the compute? With ten times the labeled data? Which would help more?

#Where to go next

  • Go deeper on the foundations: Andrej Karpathy's Neural Networks: Zero to Hero builds backpropagation and language models from scratch in code.
  • More vision, more practice: fast.ai's Practical Deep Learning for Coders trains strong image models quickly and covers deployment; Stanford's CS231n has the full lecture notes and assignments for convolutional networks.
  • Beyond classification: the Hugging Face Computer Vision Course covers vision transformers, detection, segmentation, and multimodal models with current libraries.
  • Read a landmark paper: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (He et al., 2015) introduced the ResNet you fine-tuned in Module 6. With what you know now, its figures and tables are readable.
